title: 2ஆம் பத்து, இமையவரம்பன் நெடுஞ்சேரலாதன்
theme: The second ten, Kumattur Kannanar's songs for Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan: the felling of the enemy's guardian kadamba at sea told as Murugan's killing of Sur, the drum made from that tree, enemy lands ruined against the guarded land that flowers, the queen left waiting while the king stays in camp, and a giver who will not fail even when the rains do; the preface adds his parents, the Himalayan bow and the binding of the Yavanas.
source_issues: 11-20: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the thurais are paadaan forms, and all but 19 are marked paadaan here. The patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
19: the colophon thurai is பரிசிற்றுறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு, but the poem asks for no gift; it describes the march, the war-drum rite and ravaged farmland, so it is marked vanji here.
13 lines 1-2: words are run together without spaces (தொறுத்தவயல் ஆரல்பிறழ்நவும், ஏறுபொருதசெறு உழாதுவித்துநவும்); the division is the reader's.
16 line 17 repeats 14 line 11 (எழுமுடி கெழீஇய திருஞெமர் அகலத்து) apart from the sandhi ப்; the repeated_line flag lists 16 and 40 but misses 14.
18 lines 8-10 and 20 lines 24-25 share the drought formula (மன்உயிர் அழிய யாண்டுபல ... தண்இயல் எழிலி தலையா...), with துளக்கி / மாறித் varying; not flagged.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 15 lines 33 and 37, 19 line 12, 20 line 22; the repaired readings are plausible.
patikam:2 line 14 (குமட்டூர்க் கண்ணனார் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line, as the ingest notes say.
20 line 10 has a comma inside the line (கனவினும், ஒன்னார்) where the sentence begun in line 9 ends; harmless.

reading: The poet tells Cheralathan, whose army kills in war and who drinks strained toddy, that just as Murugan, reaching the great sea, cut down Sur at the root and rode his elephant, the king went to the sea, turned the dark backwater red with the blood of the foes his spears tore open, and felled at the root the guarded kadamba that many had tended, and so the poet delights to see his much-praised wealth as he rides his tusker with its gold-ornamented neck, the king who broke the valour of every ruler from the Himalaya of the Aryans to Kumari in the south.
nuance: Line 5 (சூருடை முழுமுதல் தடிந்த) and line 13 (கடியுடை முழுமுதல் துமிய) are built on the same words, so the felling of the enemy's guardian kadamba is told as a repetition of the god's killing of Sur; the simile is the frame of the deed, not decoration. The red backwater like vermilion paste (line 10) is the only colour in the battle; the closing lines reach from the Himalaya to Kumari, the usual measure of a Tamil king's claim.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's wealth and victory as he sees it

comparisons.tenor: the king who felled the enemy's kadamba at sea and rides his elephant
the dark backwater reddened by the blood of the wounded

reading: The poet tells the king who cut the kadamba at its root, making rival kings tremble, that as the herds of other beasts quake when the maned lion walks the slope, so kings in their drum-loud towns cannot sleep for his fame, which is sweet to hear; and that his feasting is sweet to share, for the poet's large hungry kin, brought over many hills where a young elephant fans off bees beside its mother, have eaten fat meat cut with the knife, white rice with mutton and clear toddy until their old hunger ended, put off rags like a wet kite's wing, wrapped on fine cloth, and seen their women adorned with jewels.
nuance: The poem is built on two parallel predicates, கேட்டற்கு இனிது (line 9: sweet to hear) and நுகர்தற்கு இனிது (line 25: sweet to enjoy): the king's fame is a terror for kings and a feast for bards, and the same wealth is meant by both. தொல்பசி (line 15), an old, inherited hunger, makes the gift the end of a condition, not a meal.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's fame and of the feast he gave the bard's kin

comparisons.vehicle: அரிமான் வழங்கும் சாரல் பிறமான் தோடுகொள் இனநிரை
comparisons.tenor: rival kings who cannot sleep for the king's fame

reading: The poet contrasts the lands the king entered in anger, once rich watered country where bulls sowed unploughed fields, buffaloes waded among sugarcane and neythal, and old cows grazed on water-lilies by the dancing grounds, now a waste like a body Death has seized, where a ghoul-woman rides a demon over thorny scrub and the dust of empty commons, with his own guarded land, where forests are for the gods, pastures for warriors and their women, families are protected, Venus keeps its course, rain falls where it is wanted, and disease and hunger have left, so that the land flowers.
nuance: The poem sets the same kind of country twice, destroyed and flourishing, and the hinge is the king's anger (நீ சிவந்து இறுத்த, line 12) against his guarding (நீ காத்த, line 28). Lines 25 and 26 take the sky as witness: Venus not straying and rain coming on demand are signs of good rule, not luck.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king through the fate of the lands he ruins and the land he guards

comparisons.tenor: the rich land laid waste by the king's invasion

reading: The poet tells the king that he is as beyond measure as earth, water, wind and sky, as bright as the stars, planets, moon, sun and fire joined in one light, as open-handed as Akkuran who fought beside the hundred, unshakable even if Death came in anger, the shield of the worthy, husband of a queen whose beauty rivals the celestial women, ploughman whose plough is his army, king of the singing woman, and wishes that like the first kings of his line who ruled the whole sea-bounded earth he may stand with undying fame as long as this world.
nuance: The opening counts the elements as four, not five, and gives the light its own list of five (stars, planets, moon, sun, fire); the king is matched to the sky's sum, not to one body in it. படைஏர் உழவ (line 17) turns the army into a plough, the war king pictured as a farmer. The poem says nothing of Akkuran beyond his fight among the hundred.

thinai_evidence.note: a catalogue of the king's qualities ending in a blessing

comparisons.vehicle: நாள்கோள் திங்கள் ஞாயிறு கனைஅழல் ஐந்(து)ஒருங்கு புணர்ந்த விளக்கத்(து)

comparisons.tenor: the king who works his army as a ploughman works his plough
the king's lasting rule and fame

reading: The poet tells Cheralathan that he has seen the lands of the enemies who forgot his might and opposed him, where his army camped year after year, burned the outposts, broke the walls' trees and turned the old towns to waste, so that white-flowered velai, gourd and peer creepers spread over the dry tank-beds and old houses and only base men with stinking bows walk there; and that he has also seen with wonder the king's own good land of sea, hill and river, with its unfailing festivals, its drums, its blessing bards and the worthy who keep from hell and live free of distress under his care, and so he has come, loving his many qualities and his fame like Nediyon's.
nuance: The poem is told as two sights, கண்டுவந் திசினே (line 15) and கண்டுமதி மருண்டனென் (line 34): the poet's eye witnesses both the ruin and the plenty, so the praise rests on what he saw, not on report. The guarded land is defined by its people (bards who bless the world, the worthy who shun hell) as much as by its riches.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet reports what he saw of the ruined and the guarded lands to praise the king

reading: Because the king has lingered long in his war camp, where young elephants with tusks blunted from breaking the tall gates of fortress walls hung with the ayyavi roar in musth, the poet has come to see him, and asks whether the bed of his queen, of settled chastity and gentle grace, who speaks sweetly even when she sulks and has every right to think of him, will escape its loneliness, since his soft chest, bright with gems, gold and diamonds and the garland of seven crowns, which could be the bed where her eyes sleep, now torments her.
nuance: A puram poem that turns at line 10 to the queen's waiting: the same jewelled chest that wears the seven crowns' garland (line 17, as in 14 line 11) is her pillow and the cause of her pain. பூணா ஐயவி (line 4) separates the ayyavi of the siege from the white mustard a new mother wears, a pun on one word. Lines 14 and 18 to 19 are hard to construe, so the reading of the queen's lines is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet comes to the war camp to see and praise the king

reading: The poet tells the king of the green ornament, king of the singing woman, that nothing can be found to match him, since he accepts the tribute of foes who bow even when they are at fault; his great victorious drum, made from the kadamba he cut down after driving back the sea, is beaten by armleted drummers after offerings are scattered, and his sky-touching white umbrella, under rain-clouds and wheeling winds, proclaims to the wide world that has found no other refuge: come to this shade.
nuance: The drum is made of the enemy's felled guardian tree, so every beating of it repeats the victory of 11 and 12. The umbrella's call, வருக இந் நிழல் (line 9), makes the king's protection an open invitation rather than a conquest.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as without equal, by his drum and umbrella

reading: Drink the toddy, cook the rice, cut the meat, set the stew on the fire, give to all who come without limit while the gold vessels clink, let the dancing women with dark curling hair serve from the hearths, and share what you have received without fault, the poet tells the bards, for even if the cloud that has taken on the care of the earth fails for many years and the rain lies, Cheralathan will not betray their hope.
nuance: The commands are to the bards, not the king: the gift is to be passed on at once (பெற்றது உதவுமின், line 7), so the king's giving becomes the bards' hospitality. The rain is not a model he equals but one he outdoes, since rain can fail.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's unfailing giving

comparisons.tenor: Cheralathan's giving, which does not fail

reading: The poet tells the king that, with his plundering goblin-like scouts cutting through the stony road, his warriors drawing spears from tiger-skin sheaths, and his drummers beating the war drum after an offering of red millet mixed with blood, he so loves the work of war with his companions who never take off their armour that he grants no grace even to his modest, bright-browed wife, who lives with him only in dreams on the rare night he sleeps; and that the lands he ravaged, where he forbade the plough and the people fled, once had lotus and water-lily in every pond, neythal in the paddy, reapers' sickles bending and sugar presses groaning, so that onlookers clap their hands in pity, saying these were good only yesterday, and many fine lands have come to nothing.
nuance: The colophon calls this a song of the gift (பரிசிற்றுறை), but the poem asks for nothing: it sets the king's love of war against two losses, his wife's and the ravaged farmers'. The onlookers' words (lines 24 and 25) are the poem's only voice of grief. The syntax of lines 9 to 15 (who is pitied, and by whom) is hard, and the reading of the wife's lines is tentative.

thinai_evidence.note: the army's march, the war-drum rite and the ravaging of enemy farmland

reading: If you ask who our king is, says the poet, he is Neduncheralathan, who went against his foes on an island in the sea and cut down the kadamba at its root: may his garland live; his deeds against enemies never failed by a mote of sunlit dust, he is false neither in enemy land nor even in dreams, he crushed the proud and stormed moated, walled forts, he scatters horses, elephants and chariots to drummers and players without stint, and with a heart that does not swerve in the duty of giving, to our people or others, skilled or unskilled, he will not let a belly go hungry even if the rains fail for many years: may the womb of the mother who bore him be free of blemish.
nuance: The poem is shaped as an answer to a stranger's question (நும்கோ யார், line 1), the form a bard uses to send another to his patron. The blessing falls not on the king but on his mother's womb (line 27), so the praise ends by honouring where he came from. Truthfulness is claimed even in dreams (கனவினும், line 10).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's truthfulness and giving

comparisons.tenor: the king's giving, which does not fail

reading: The decade's preface says that Imayavaramban Neduncheralathan, son of Udhiyan Cheral of the sweet-sounding drum by Nallini of the Veliyan Vel line, carved his bow on the Himalaya, set up his rule so that the sea-fenced Tamil land shone, made the Aryans bow, bound the harsh-spoken Yavanas, poured ghee on their heads and tied their hands behind them, took their costly vessels and diamonds to his old city and gave to others, and that Kumattur Kannanar sang this ten.
nuance: The preface supplies what the songs leave out: the king's parents, the Himalayan bow and the humiliation of the Yavanas. The seized treasure is at once given away (பிறர்க்கு உதவி, line 11), the same pairing of conquest and gift as in 12 and 20.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's lineage, conquests and giving

comparisons.tenor: the sea that bounds the Tamil land

title: 3ஆம் பத்து, பல்யானைச் செல்கெழு குட்டுவன்
theme: The third ten, Palai Gauthamanar's songs for Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan: the king's sacrifices and open kitchen, the faults that block dharma's wheel, the bards he feeds in drought, the six-duty Brahmins whose word he follows, a series of enemy lands seen at their height and ruined by his anger, his own land watered even in drought, and the great rice offering before battle; the preface adds his conquests and his last journey to the forest.
source_issues: 21-30: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai. 22, 23, 25, 26, 27, 29 and 30 are marked vanji here by their content (ravaged or threatened enemy land, the pre-battle rite); the colophons say paadaan forms except 30.
29: the colophon thurai is written without a space (வஞ்சித்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு), unlike 22, 23, 25 and 26.
22 line 22: வாயிதூங்குபு looks like வாயில் தூங்குபு run together with the ல் lost.
24 line 18: உண்மருந்(து) இன்மரும் is obscure; it probably stands for those who eat and those who chew (உண்மரும் தின்மரும்), and is marked uncertain.
28 line 6: நீணதொழில் is not a clear word and may be corrupt; marked uncertain.
30 line 21: செழும்பல் வைப்பி looks like வைப்பின் with the final ன் lost.
patikam:3 line 7: நீணரும் probably stands for நீரும் (இருகடல் நீரும், the waters of the two seas).
25 line 1: the repaired word (மாஆ டியபுலன்) comes from sangamtamil.com; lines 10-12 (the drum-bearing elephant and banners) are compressed and the reading is marked uncertain.

Repeated lines flagged: 23 line 10 = 43 line 11; 28 line 9 = 43 line 14; 30 line 40 = 34 line 2. 23 lines 5-6 and 29 lines 8-9 share the bards' line-words (வயிரிய மாக்கள், மறுகுசிறை பாடும்) without a flag.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 21 lines 27 and 34, 23 lines 7 and 21, 28 line 10, 30 line 6; the repaired readings are plausible.

reading: The poet praises the Chera who, guided by the five disciplines of the learned and speaking truth as clear as daybreak, keeps two fires going at once, the oblation of the sacrifice for the gods and the roaring kitchen where fat meat is fried without stint for every guest, so that both smells rise and please even the gods in the sky; he hails him as lord of the Puzhiyar whose cowherds find gems on the rocky pasture, shield of the Mazhavar and lord of the hill Ayirai, and wishes him, with his wife of fragrant hair and wandering rain-cool eyes, countless ages of life while the rains never fail.
nuance: Lines 7 and 13 call both fires ஆவுதி: the sacrificial ghee and the cooking fat of the guests' kitchen are the same kind of offering, and line 14 has them smell together (இரண்டு உடன் கமழும்). The poem ends not on the king's war but on his queen, a rare domestic close for a decade poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's sacrifices and open kitchen and blesses him and his queen

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the frying in the kitchen

reading: The poet tells Kuttuvan, descendant of rulers who kept away anger, desire, excessive indulgence, fear, lies, too much love and harsh punishment, the obstacles to the wheel of dharma, and so led an age when no one harmed or coveted, couples were not parted, food was shared and people died old and free of disease, that he who took the Kongar's land of cows and deep rock-cut wells and broke the guarded Agappa fort with its moat, walls and bow-engines has turned his anger on a festive watered country where men dam floods to the drum, so that, pitiably, it will become a great waste where at noon the jackal howls, the owl hoots and the demoness walks.
nuance: The list of faults in lines 1-4 is of excesses on both sides: harshness (தெறல் கடுமை) sits beside excessive kindness (கழிகண்ணோட்டம்) and excess of love, so the wheel of dharma is blocked by too much mercy as well as too little. The poem then praises the lineage for this restraint and ends with the king's anger laying a land waste; the poet's அளிய (pitiable) is his only comment.

thinai_evidence.note: because the king is angry with it, the rich enemy land will become waste

reading: The bards tell Kuttuvan of the golden garland, who even in a drought when cicadas cry on the dead unnam tree and the earth has lost its green ends the hunger of the street-singing musicians and throws great jewels even at small pleasures, that on their way to him they saw the lands of the kings who fought him and fled: once watered country of marutham trees, kaanchi-lined fords, fire-red murukku, conches, herons and lotus fields, they have become sky-high forest where grass blocks the untravelled roads and the wild cow lives happily with her bull.
nuance: The drought of lines 1-3 at home is answered by the king's giving, while the enemy's land, which had no drought, is ruined by war; the two halves weigh natural against man-made ruin. The wild cow living happily with her bull is the poem's sign that the forest has truly returned: pleasure has passed from people to beasts.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards report the rich lands of kings who fought him turned to forest

reading: The poet hails the leader of a great army whose warriors raise spears drawn from tiger-skin sheaths like spreading lightning, who conducts himself by the word of the Brahmins devoted to dharma who keep the six duties of learning, sacrificing, having others do both, giving and receiving, so that the world walks his way; husband of the queen of refined speech, he is harder to measure than the five elements, and the poet has seen his swelling wealth: an unfailing rice for all comers, pounded by pestles worn ringless, with meat cut by knives in the great pots, which all marvel at, so that even if the rain-cloud forgot its season when Venus stands to the north, his wealth would keep its yield.
nuance: The king's dharma is deference: he walks by the Brahmins' word and the world walks by his (lines 8-9). The closing claim that his wealth outlasts a failed monsoon makes royal plenty independent of the rain that the ethics books tie to just rule.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's conduct, measureless greatness and wealth

comparisons.tenor: the spears raised by the warriors
the king's greatness, harder to measure

reading: The poet tells the king that in the wide lands of others where he drove his tall chariot, its banners rippling like a waterfall off a mountain and its drum roaring like thunder, the fields trodden by his horses are no longer ploughed, the ground where his musth elephants spread knows no harvest, donkeys wander the commons his soldiers camped in, fire fanned by the wind has danced over the land, and the dried forest road where the owl-headed bird roams has become a great waste.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's invasion leaves others' lands ploughless and burned

reading: The poet says that in the land the king's warriors, like a Death that nothing afflicts, have raged against, where chariots spread no plough goes, where elephants trod no plough moves, and houses that echoed with churning hear no music, he grieves when he thinks of the wealth its old inhabitants knew: they, holding back tears and beating their hands, say the rain has failed and the heat has come and that this is the nature of the times, while their fenced homes turn to ruins overgrown with peerkku and nerunji and the old town loses its festivity.
nuance: The victims blame the season (காலையது பண்பு, line 7), not the king, while the poet knows the cause and says so in a praise poem; his நோகோ யானே is the most open grief for the conquered in the decade.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet grieves over the enemy land the king's warriors ravaged

reading: The poet tells the king that surely it is ruined, since he looked at it in anger: the desirable beauty of a good land of unfailing yield, where men wearing kuvalai and ambal and drinking toddy climb the marutham by the ford to dive, peacocks dance in the field groves when bangled women call, and carts sink in the mud of the neythal-lined fields so that the oxen strain, and no uproar was known but the shouting of the carters.
nuance: Only the first line tells of ruin; the other fifteen describe the land as it was, so the king's anger is measured by what it destroyed. The only 'uproar' of the old land is carts stuck in rich mud, the figure the next poem uses for the king's own country.

thinai_evidence.note: the beauty of the enemy's watered land is ruined by the king's angry look

reading: The poet says the king's wide land is rich indeed: since he guards it so well that his warriors, who broke the paired ranks of the enemy's elephants, forget their quick archery and the harvest never fails, even in a great drought when summer lingers, the hills turn pale and the falls run dry, the flood of the great river, crowned with straw, overflows its banks into the fields, and apart from the uproar of that red water no heat is known there.
nuance: The war is present only as something forgotten (கதழ்தொடை மறப்ப): peace at home is the warriors' idleness. Line 6 (நீணதொழில்) looks corrupt, so the cause clause is read loosely.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's own land as safe and watered

reading: The poet says that the broad settlements, pitiably, used to flourish before the boundless army of Kuttuvan of many elephants spread over them, he whose fierce drum, fed with blood and mixed grain, calls him past the rules of battle to take hard forts: there bangled women rested their pestles against the plantains to pluck vallai, herons fat on ayirai fish crowded the trees above the ripe paddy and were chased off by the women, and at unceasing festivals the bards tuned their lutes and sang at the street corners.
nuance: The whole description is governed by the past-and-gone particle மன் (ஆடுமன், line 10) and by ஊங்கே, 'before', in the last line, so the poem is a portrait of a land as it was until the army came, not a picture of it now.

thinai_evidence.note: the enemy lands were happy only until the king's army spread over them

reading: The poet tells the fiercely angry king that his drum, roaring with a voice that shakes the earth like thunder, calls his never-retreating warriors to scatter the great rice, while the drum-rich kings and velir of every land, the sea shore of neythal, punnai, pearls and coral, the hills where hunters trade tusks and meat for liquor, the watered fields of sugarcane and festivals, the dry millet uplands and the sand-ridged forests, tremble though they hold forts in sea and forest; the rice ball raised by the priest for the god of the rite, a blood-soaked offering that the demoness shakes before and that even ants do not touch, is eaten by crows and kites.
nuance: Thirty lines survey every kind of land the enemies hold, sea, hill, field, upland and forest, so that the trembling of their kings at the drum (line 31) is the trembling of the whole land. The great rice is an offering before it is a meal: raised by the priest, shaken at by the demoness, left even by ants and eaten by crows and kites.

thinai_evidence.note: before the march, the king calls his warriors to the great rice offering

comparisons.tenor: the dark petals of the neythal

reading: The decade's preface says that Palyanai Selkezhu Kuttuvan, younger brother of Imayavaramban, set his sceptre over Umbarkadu, struck down Agappa, performed sacrifice with the daytime fire, took to himself the elders of moon-clear tradition, divided and gave away land, led long rows of black elephants, bathed in the two seas in one day and worshipped Ayirai, and that, of unfailing fame and high learning, he went to the forest with Nedumbarathayanar going before him; Palai Gauthamanar sang the ten.
nuance: Only the preface tells that the king ended by leaving for the forest with a Brahmin teacher; the songs show him at war and at sacrifice. Agappa and Ayirai tie the preface to 22 and 21.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's conquests, gifts and final retreat to the forest

title: 4ஆம் பத்து, களங்காய்க்கண்ணி நார்முடிச் சேரல்
theme: The fourth ten, Kappiyaatru Kappiyanar's songs for Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral: a festival of Vishnu framing the king who set the shaken peoples right, a conqueror not angry in the enemy's land, an army that is its own fortress, the blood-field as the king's unfailing wealth, an unbent rule beside victory, a king who will not eat sweet things alone, and a dancer guided to the slayer of Nannan, who gives war elephants; the preface adds his birth, the Poozhi conquest and Nannan's beheading.
source_issues: 31-40: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); 33 is marked vanji, 34 and 39 thumbai, 35 and 36 vaakai, the rest paadaan. 39's colophon says வாகை, but the poem's matter is the thumbai battle and the forts that wither.
31 line 25 was supplied from sangamtamil.com (flag: eye-skip in our source joined two lines).
33 line 1 reads இறும்பூதால் பரிதே, but the decade's linked openings repeat 32's last line, இறும்பூதால் பெரிதே; பரிதே is likely a misprint.
33 line 6 நரிதரும் is probably a misprint for நெரிதரும் (crushing); the line is read that way here.
34 line 8 is a lacuna (dots in the source); 34 line 10 முரை(சு) is likely a misprint for முர(சு).
37 line 7 துளங்குடி for துளங்குகுடி (32 line 7, patikam line 12) looks like a dropped syllable; 37 line 9 தாணஇத் is unclear and may be corrupt.
36 line 8 and 39 line 10 share the line பொறித்த போலும் புள்ளி எருத்தின் (flagged), applied to a vulture in 36 and to doves in 39.
Repaired lines (flags): 32 line 17 (TSCII leftover) and 40 line 4 (stray space); both readings are plausible.
patikam:4 line 14 (காப்பியாற்றுக் காப்பியனார் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.

reading: The poet sets the king among scenes of a sacred festival, where fasting crowds from the four quarters, to the clang of bells, bathe at the cold ghat and praise the red feet of the lord with the tulasi garland and the discus before going home glad, and tells him that like the full moon driving off the dark he set the shaken peoples right and took the drum, that his chest is like the cloud-soaked mountain and his shoulders like the bar of the sky fortress, that he is like the rich and famous Vandan, that his queen is like the red star among the women of the sky, and that his army, which never strikes a fleeing back, is a shield to friends and a terror to foes.
nuance: The first ten lines are a festival of Vishnu with no word yet about the king; the poem then turns to him through the moon simile, so the worshippers' joy at the god's feet becomes the frame for the people's relief under the king. The queen is praised in the same breath as his body and army (lines 23 to 28), as the red star (செம்மீன்) that tradition names Arundhati, the model of chastity. Line 33 (புறக்கொடை எறியார்) states the rule of not striking a fleeing back as a trait of his soldiers.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's rule, body, queen and army

comparisons.tenor: the king who set the shaken peoples right, as the full moon drives off the dark

comparisons.vehicle: தூங்(கு)எயில் கதவம் காவல் கொண்ட எழூஉநிவந்(து) அன்ன

comparisons.tenor: the king, rich and famous through the world
the queen of the old city, chief in chastity
the king's army as it falls on enemies

reading: The poet says the king's virtues are too many to count, his fame and rectitude that light the quarters, his wealth that gives until it is spent so that his kin rejoice, and the victory that set the shaken peoples right, yet one thing amazes him: having broken the enemy's strength and camped with mountain-like elephants to ruin their land, and having taken their country of sure harvests where the heron feeds in the paddy among canes, the king is not angry even in the land of those foes who reviled him.
nuance: The praise turns on restraint, not ferocity: the conquest is told in a few lines so that the closing wonder (இறும்பூதால் பெரிதே) can fall on the absence of anger where it could be used. The counting pebbles failing (இடுகழங்கு தபுந, line 8) is a counting game used as a measure of the king's virtues.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's virtues and one wonder in particular

reading: The poet tells the lord of the bannered chariot that, when his army ties its belled, palm-legged elephants to the enemy's guardian tree, muddies the deep fords and camps all around like an endless flood that ruins the land, it is itself a fortress, with swords for its wall, raised spears for its thorn hedge, the red points of arrows for its moat and drums that roar like thunder, a fort that moves on foot, and kings who would face him in war shrink from him once they think of it.
nuance: The poem builds a fortress out of the marching army, part by part, so the king who breaks walls needs none of his own. Tying war elephants to the enemy's guarded tree (கடிமரம்) is the insult that opens the war; the decade's preface tells how the king cut down Nannan's guardian vakai.

thinai_evidence.note: the army marches into enemy land, camps and ties its elephants to the guardian tree

comparisons.tenor: the strong legs of the elephants
the army as a fortress of swords, spears and arrows
the roar of the war drums

reading: The poet says kings shun the great king because, when warriors with anklets and robes trailing to the ground come on red-maned horses, on long-bannered chariots and on the necks of gold-decked elephants with blazing forehead plates, he wears down the stand of unyielding men, breaks the great drummed battle amid rising shouts and overcomes kings, and so the noble young man guards his people.
nuance: Line 8 is a gap in the text, so what the warriors of lines 2 to 7 are set against is lost; the chain of three mounts (horse, chariot, elephant) gives the three arms of the enemy force before the gap. The last line (ஓம்பல் மாறே) gives guarding as the reason for the victories, and is the line the next poem begins from.

thinai_evidence.note: the clash of two kings' armies and the king's power to overcome them

reading: The poet says the king's victories are worth telling: on the wide field where great elephants lie with their shining tusks, chariot wheels have run over them and crested birds will not go in with their flocks, where headless bodies dance on the battleground and the square of blood glows red like the evening sky, demons dance, and that conquering war is his unfailing wealth.
nuance: The closing line calls the blood-field itself the king's unfailing abundance (வீயா யாணர்), a word used of fertile land; the battlefield is praised as a field that never stops yielding. The dancing headless bodies (மெய்ஆடு, line 6) are the கவந்தம் of later war poetry.

thinai_evidence.note: the victor's battlefield is praised as his wealth

reading: The poet tells the king, whose wealth never fails, that with a glad heart he overcame fresh battles at the head of mighty warriors, and in the fierce vanguard where swords clashed many elephants fell with their trunks cut like palms in a cleared field, the grey-backed vulture with its mate and spotted neck and the hawk carried off the flesh of fallen horses and men, fearsome demons bearing long rows of the dead ate and danced in joy, and red blood ran, so he makes many wars; long live his wealth.
nuance: The cleared palm field (பனைதடி புனம், line 5) turns the felled elephants into farm work, as the kalavazhi thurai, named after the threshing floor, tends to do. The male vulture paired with its mate (பெடைபுணர் சேவல்) keeps a love-poem image in a scene of carrion.

thinai_evidence.note: the slaughter of the field is told to the victor

comparisons.tenor: elephants felled with their trunks cut
the spotted neck of the vulture

reading: The poet blesses the king's wealth and life, as truthful men praise his fame: he gives grief in full to enemies and scatters fine jewels in full to friends, a restrained and calm chief without fault whose fame breathes with the world; he has the victory that set the shaken peoples right, wears the dark palm garland and great anklets, breaks kings' forts and upholds his warriors, and keeps an unbending rule set straight for those who live in his shade; this the fierce king has in great measure for the people of the world.
nuance: Lines 3 and 4 balance in one pattern (பகைவர் ஆர / நகைவர் ஆர): grief for foes and gifts for friends are given in the same full measure. The rule is described with the bending metaphor twice over (கோடற வைத்த கோடாக் கொள்கை), so straightness is set beside the victory as a second possession.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's victory and his straight rule

comparisons.tenor: the king's protection of those who live under him

reading: The poet says many in the world are rich but the king's fame exceeds them all, Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral who set right the country where wealth had been thrown into confusion, lord of elephants with ringed tusks and red-maned horses, king of the Cheras, the wealth of suppliants, the day-court of bards, husband of the bright-browed queen, bull among warriors, of scarred and spotless chest, Vaanavaramban, because, with a heart free of the flaw that wishes sweet things to be given so each may enjoy them alone, he has gathered the manliness of sharing food and lives for others.
nuance: Sharing food is called manliness (பகுத்(து)ஊண் தொகுத்த ஆண்மை), placed among the war titles as one more of them. Lines 5 and 6 may play on தோட்டி, the goad that drives the elephant against the fort gate and perhaps also the name of the fort it won; the second sense cannot be settled from this text.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's fame and his living for others

comparisons.tenor: the king as the wealth of suppliants

reading: The poet says that because the king lives for others, the band who tell his valour never say they lack anything: in the hot thumbai battle, while the war drum roars like thunder, the guarded front of the angry foes cries out and the forts of the unyielding wither as he goes, fierce as Death; and in the mantle of green gold set with gems, woven not of thread but fine as hair, bright as lightning and sewn with pearls, like the spider's web hung on the dry branches of the velam tree where the flock of grey-backed, spotted-necked doves cries, they delight in the shade of his war.
nuance: The syntax of lines 9 to 16 is hard: the gold mesh that is like a spider's web on a thorn tree seems to be the king's war mantle, and the crying doves are the frightened enemy's land, but the connection of the parts is not certain. The shade of war (போர்நிழல்) that the band delights in is the next poem's opening.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's fury in the thumbai battle against unsubmissive forts

comparisons.tenor: the spotted neck of the doves

reading: Praying that the king's army, which with its kin delights in the shade of war, may never turn back from a town's front, the poet tells how it camped in ripe fields where karanthai spread, silenced the warriors of the kings' forts, killed and won the hard battle of crowned kings, filled the people and danced the victory, under Narmudi Cheral who cut down at the guarded root the flame-flowered vakai of Nannan of the golden chariot, who rejoices in the toddy he gives while strained liquor holds back suppliants, lord of Neri hill; and he tells the small-bangled dancer that if she goes, adorned like the flowering vengai, with bards in fresh flowers and young men praising the wide field, he will give her many trained war elephants.
nuance: The guide poem gives the dancer war elephants, not jewels or food: the spoils of the battle in the first half are what the patron hands out in the second. Line 17 (புன்கால் உன்னம் சாய) names the unnam tree, which droops as an omen of defeat for the king's foes. The felling of Nannan's vakai (line 15) is the deed the decade's preface makes its centre.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem guides a dancer to the king who will give elephants

reading: The decade's preface says that Kalangaaykkanni Narmudi Cheral, son of Cheralathan of unfailing fortune by the queen of Padhuman, lord of the Vel Aavi line, was born to make the battle front tremble, grew in fame, took the Poozhi country by war, cut off the head of Nannan of Peruvaayil in a pitched battle, felled the whole trunk of his gold-bearing vakai, made the red flood of blood drag elephants, fought many battles, performed the sacrifice of the red field and set the shaken peoples right; and that Kappiyaatru Kappiyanar sang this ten.
nuance: The preface supplies what the songs only touch: his parentage, the Poozhi conquest and the killing of Nannan, which 40 mentions only through the felled vakai. The battlefield sacrifice (செங்களம் வேட்டு) and the shaken peoples set right (துளங்குகுடி திருத்திய) repeat the songs' own formulas (32, 37).

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's birth and conquests

title: 5ஆம் பத்து, கடல் பிறக்கோட்டிய செங்குட்டுவன்
theme: The fifth ten, Paranar's songs for Kadal Pirakkottiya Senguttuvan: the bard's hard road to the king whose feet toiled at sea, scarred warriors and horses beyond counting, gifts like drought-breaking rain, the war at Mohur for a distant kinsman and the neem made into a drum, a king without equal who drove back the sea, performers who never take their leave, slaughter that is itself a gift, a name to outlast the river sands, a virali guided by the Mohur slaughter, and the sleepless king in camp; the preface adds the northern expedition for the Pattini stone and the Chola wars.
source_issues: 41-50: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); 50 is marked vanji for its war camp and the preface vanji for the northern expedition, the rest paadaan.
41: show flags a line after the colophon kept in colophon_raw, not verse. Line 11 சேஎர் is unclear (the Chera people, or சேர் 'reach').

42 line 9 தாணஇ and 50 lines 10, 23, 26 வொணஇய, மாணஇப், மாணஇய look like encoding leftovers (ணஇ for a long vowel sign); 50 line 9 மன்ண is probably a misprint for மின்ன (flashing). 50 line 8 has a stray comma inside the line.
42 line 21 and 46 line 11 spell பெளவம் with ெ + ள rather than the vowel sign ௌ.
44 line 8 காணிலியரோ and lines 18 and 22-23 are hard to construe; 44 line 1 துடையூ is unusual and may be corrupt.
Repaired lines (flags): 42 line 23, 43 line 4, 46 line 13, 48 line 10, 49 line 5 and patikam:5 line 6; all repaired readings are plausible.
48 line 9 (வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை) is repeated at 70 line 20, and 49 line 5 at 81 line 7 (flagged).
patikam:5 line 23 (காசறு செய்யுட் பரணர் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.

reading: The poet tells how his band of young performers, carrying lute, drums and horns packed in their bundles and praising the god, crossed many dry tracks of a forest where rain has failed and the bamboo withers, where a mighty elephant, taking a sound for the roar of a tiger pack, tears down a branch of flame-flowered vengai and wears it on its head like warriors of the army meeting battle, staff in hand; he has come to see the faultless lord of the strong chariot, and he asks whether the king's feet, which rode the swift maned horse and toiled in the cold sea of crashing waves, can be free of weariness, the feet of a king whose one-word warriors fulfilled their vows, broke kings in drum-loud battle and pounded enemy heads as pestles pound pepper.
nuance: The poem is in two halves: the hardship of the road the poet bore to see the king, and then the hardship the king's own feet bore at sea, so the bard's journey and the king's campaign are set against each other. The question தாவல் உய்யுமோ (line 17) is a turn of courtesy, concern for the king's feet, that becomes praise of the campaign. The elephant that mistakes something for a tiger and attacks the vengai rests on the old pairing of the vengai's flowers with the tiger's stripes.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet has crossed the dry road to see the king and praises him on sight

comparisons.vehicle: செல்படை மறவர் தண்(டு)உடை வலத்தர் போர்எதிர்ந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: the elephant wearing the torn vengai branch and trumpeting

reading: The poet hails Kuttuvan, husband of the fair-browed queen and lord of men who wear the dark palmyra garland and anklets of giving, whose chests are deeply scarred where the long white needle went in and out like a kingfisher diving into a cold pool for fish and rising again, and who wear the thumbai only beside men whose bodies have taken arrows; after each battle won he puts on a fresh garland strewn with inji flowers, pours sweet gem-coloured wine from sandal-smeared jars with unsparing joy so that the great kin of the performers thrive, and the prancing maned horses he has showered on them, if counted, are more than the cold waves of the dark clear sea that come crashing in white-crested spray.
nuance: The scar is the warrior's credential: thumbai is worn only with those already wounded, so courage is counted on the body before the gift is counted in horses. The kingfisher simile is of the surgeon's needle sewing the wound, the bird's dive and rise matching the needle's passage through the flesh.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's warriors and of his gifts of horses

comparisons.vehicle: மீன்தேர் கொட்பின் பனிக்கயம் மூழ்கிச் சிரல்பெயர்ந் தன்ன
comparisons.tenor: the long needle passing in and out of the warriors' wounds
the horses the king has given

reading: The poet hails Kuttuvan of the gold garland, whose slaying army broke in shouting battle the drum-rich kings between the Himalaya, the god-haunted high mountain of the north where women with chowrie tufts swing and the musth tuskers come with she-elephants beyond counting, and Kumari in the south, and spoiled the old beauty of lands of many tongues; as in a drought, when palmyras wither, hills go dry and falls stop, the roaring sky pours rain with thunder and breaks the banks of the great river while ploughmen wearing konrai yoke their ploughs, so he lets the ascetics eat their fill, scatters jewels to the merry, and bids that the singing viralis get many she-elephants, the plundering warriors get killing tuskers and the herald who praises the field get horses; since he loves war, even his foes praise him, and the poet has seen his state at feasts where the fat-smoke fire never dies and the toddy never fails the musicians.
nuance: The rain is not the ordinary rain of the season but rain that breaks a drought, so the king's gift is measured against need, not against plenty. The roll of gifts is graded by receiver: she-elephants to the singing women, war tuskers to the fighters, horses to the herald, each gift fitted to its use.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's conquests and of his giving to every kind of suppliant

comparisons.tenor: the king's giving to every suppliant

reading: The poet hails the lord of swaying gait whose victorious banner touches the sky on his chariot amid a roar like the earth being struck, who flings away unsparingly what he won in battle without calling it rare, and has never known even in dream to say 'hold back': for the sake of Arukai of the fine uzhinai, whom he called kin though far off and who had fled his land in an unended feud, he stormed the fort like one possessed, took the drum of the king of Mohur, humbled his boast, cut down his neem at the root, yoked many elephants to drag it for a drum, on the Kuraalam field where tufted owls cry and the crossroads grieve; he drove off many drum-rich kings, and his land is the one where the vanni common holds the urns that hid kings who once ruled the wide earth.
nuance: The war is told as a friend's duty: the king fights Mohur because Arukai, distant though he is, was declared kin (சேணன் ஆயினும் கேள்என மொழிந்து). The felled guardian neem becomes the victor's own war drum, so the enemy's sacred tree is made to sound his victories. Line 8, காணிலியரோ, and the burial urns of the last lines are hard to construe.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving and of his war at Mohur

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the king's army

reading: The poet asks whether there are now, or were before, any kings like this Cheral, who wears the gold thumbai and the chest-garland won from seven crowns, whose arrows lie quiet in the spotted quiver like snakes in an anthill, whose bow bends and heart does not, whose spears are notched from striking elephants; who crossed the deep-moated walls of forts that others had sacked and enjoyed of old, raised his land-winning shoulders like the bars that guard a gate, danced the thunangai on the corpse-heaped field, fed meat-paste rice to men who never retreat, and threw his spear to drive back the roaring cold sea that rain clouds do not empty nor rivers fill.
nuance: The sea that neither shrinks when clouds drink from it nor swells when rivers enter (lines 19, 20) is the image of what cannot be moved, and the king moves it; the sea-repelling feat that gives the decade's king his name is here the climax of a list of land battles. The question 'are there such now? none before you either' makes the praise historical: he is measured against all past kings.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as without equal among kings past and present

comparisons.tenor: the arrows resting in the quiver

reading: Because Kuttuvan of victorious fame, lord of killing elephants who crossed many battles cutting countless heads, whose chariot wheel runs over many wastes, and who threw his spear to drive back the conch-loud sea of breaking waves, protects them well and pours sweet joy on them, the women in jewels, ear-rings and cool garlands, with bright bangles and gem-lit breasts and bee-haunted hair, tune the great lute to the paalai mode and sing the uzhinai of his unbowing line; those who have seen him never say 'we will go', and move about only singing.
nuance: The praise works by an absence: the performers never speak the word of leave-taking (செல்குவம் என்னார்), which in other gift poems is the moment the bard departs rewarded. The women sing a war theme, uzhinai, in the paalai mode of the lute, a music named for the parting land.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king whose bounty keeps the performers from leaving

reading: Kuttuvan never tires of slaying, and each time he slays the suppliants never tire of receiving elephants; and in his ancient city, where banners wave in the wind from the mansions like falls pouring down a mountain, where the big lamps on their stands burn with broad flames fed from ghee-dripping spouts, and bright-browed viralis dance, the talk of him never ends.
nuance: The eight lines are built on one verb repeated three times, ஆனான், ஆனார், ஆனா: the king's killing, the suppliants' gain and the city's talk of him are made one unbroken chain, so that each slaughter is at once a gift.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's slaying and of the suppliants' unending gain

comparisons.tenor: the banners rippling from the mansions

reading: The poet blesses the name of the king who crowns the bards with gold lotuses and hangs necklaces on the bright-browed viralis, who set his imperishable fame by entering the water and toiling with the sea, lord of the paravar of the cold shore, of whom his skilled attendants say as they stand in rows that he gives here easily, even to songs that ask nothing, the treasure he took there at sea, a man of truth who never learned otherwise; gentle in bearing and unbending in manhood, his many-spotted chest has lost its garland and sandal to the fire that burns the enemy front; may his name live longer than the sands of the great Kaanchi ford where bands bathe in the sweet water born on his mountains and rushing to his sea, at the festival where kin enjoy a summer life in the groves.
nuance: The king is addressed as lord of the fishermen (பனித்துறைப் பரதவ) because of his sea war, and the river that runs from his mountain to his sea makes the whole land, hill to shore, his. வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை (line 9) pairs a bowing gentleness with an unbowing manhood; the line recurs in 70. Whether காஞ்சி names a river or the kaanchi trees of the ford is not settled by the poem.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's nature is told and his name blessed

comparisons.tenor: the years the king's name should live

reading: The speaker calls the viralis of swaying gait and drooping garlands to come along with him so that their kin who live by song may eat well, for he has seen Kuttuvan of great anger, who, when kings and Velir agreed together and came crowding to Mohur swollen with strength, with elephants spreading, horses held in, banners gleaming and chariots wheeling, charged so that the massed array shook, while red-handed warriors' blood ran over the ground like a rain-day flood filling the hollows, corpses heaped up, the drum roared in the middle, the place was ruined and many dwellers died, and he cut down the victorious neem of dark branches.
nuance: The guide does not describe the gifts at all, only the slaughter at Mohur: the proof that the viralis will eat well is the scale of the king's victory. The blood-flood simile borrows the rain image of plenty for the field of the dead.

thinai_evidence.note: a performer guides the viralis to the king

comparisons.tenor: the blood running over the battlefield

reading: The poet tells the king that he is like the confluence where the Kaveri, flowing due east in muddy flood and fed by rains that thunder like mountains, scatter hail and make the deer herds tremble, enrich the cane-fields and sustain the world, joins two more flowery streams; having crossed battles at forts on hills and by the sea, taken the enemy's land and filled his foes with dread, he asks how the many days pass for the great one whose eyes, in the camp where hatred of the enemy keeps him, cannot even take a short hard-won sleep and are woken by the roar of horns, when he might lie embraced on the soft pillow of women's loosened hair, their sandal and colour rubbed away and bees humming on their breasts.
nuance: The poem praises endurance by naming what the king gives up: the embrace is drawn in akam detail and then set aside for the camp's broken sleep, so the king's love is the measure of his resolve. Lines 8 to 10 are partly corrupt (மன்ண, வொணஇய), and the sense of the army as a flood that is the kings' fortress is a guess.

thinai_evidence.note: the king is on campaign in the war camp, taking the enemy's country

reading: The decade's preface says that Senguttuvan, who drove back the sea, son of Nedum Cheralathan, lord of the westerners whose sky-touching banner the northerners fear, by the Chola Manakkilli, went through the forests by the arrow to take a stone for the goddess Pattini, defeated the Aryan lord, bathed it in the far-famed Ganga of sweet falls, brought back herds of cows with their calves, camped outside Idumbil, cut down Viyalur where warriors like tigers fell, reached the far bank and destroyed Kodukur, felled the whole trunk of the dark neem guarded by Pazhaiyan, yoked it to an elephant cart with ropes of the hair of his many wives, who had put off their jewels, killed nine of the Chola line in endless battle, camped at their gate and broke their standing strength; and that Paranar of flawless verse sang this ten.
nuance: The preface tells what the songs leave out: the northern expedition for the Pattini stone and the Chola wars. It also names whose neem was felled (Pazhaiyan's) and the ropes that dragged it, the hair of his widowed wives, which the songs (44, 49) only touch on.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface tells the northern expedition and the wars that followed

title: 6ஆம் பத்து, ஆடுகோட் பாட்டுச் சேரலாதன்
theme: The sixth ten, Kakkaipadiniyar Nachchellaiyar's songs for Adukotpattu Cheralathan: a king soft-seeming at home and like Death in battle, a hand that only gives, a war elephant that would charge his own city's gate, a giver who should forgo heaven and rest like a cloud after rain, the dance motif turned three ways (the queen's anger at the thunangai, the denial of festival skill, the victory dance on the field), virali guide poems, and the king's duty to keep the roads open; the preface ties his name to seized goats and his title Vaanavaramban to a gift.
source_issues: 51-60: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai. All are marked paadaan here except 56 (vaakai, by its ஒள்வாள் அமலை victory dance).
தாணஇயர் (52 lines 3 and 28, 53 line 1, 58 line 4) and தாணஇப் (53 line 15) look like unrepaired TSCII leftovers for தரீஇயர் / தரீஇ; they are not flagged.
55 line 10: வேணடித் is a misprint for வேண்டித்.
51 line 14 and 55 line 3: பெளவத்து is written with ெ + ள rather than ௌ (பௌவத்து); an encoding variant.
57 line 6 and 60 line 3: செல்லா மோதில் is spaced as two words that should be read செல்லாமோ தில், as Purananuru 64 line 2 has it.
53 spells the thurai செந்துறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு with a space; 55, 58 and 59 write செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு without.
Repeated lines flagged: 58 lines 3 and 19 (with 67 and 66), 59 line 12 (with 62), patikam:6 lines 10 and 14; repaired TSCII lines flagged in 51 (2, 36), 53 (9), 59 (16), 60 (4, 10) read plausibly.
patikam:6 line 14 is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.

reading: The poet tells the king that because he lingers in his cool sea-coast land, where the palmyra grove sways like a possessed girl dancing and the viralis sing to him, those who do not know him may think the lord of the white spear is gentle; but he is like the thunderbolt that strikes the angry snake on the cloud-hung hill, and his look in battle, where his spearmen cut the tusks of elephants and the drums torn by arrows fall silent, is Death spreading its net.
nuance: The poem turns on a mistaken impression (மெல்லியன் போன்ம், line 23): the long, lush seaside description of lines 1 to 22 is the evidence the unknowing would use, and the second half answers it with two similes of sudden killing, the thunder and Death's net. The softness is not denied; it is placed at home. Lines 12 to 16 (gems, snakes, conches, the canopy between the eastern and western seas) are compressed and their syntax is hard to fix.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's terror in battle against his gentle look at home

comparisons.tenor: the opened neythal flowers, like eyes
the king, who strikes like the thunderbolt that kills the snake

reading: The poet says she has heard that the king's hand, which won the good war when his elephants and chariots spread into foreign land like a great ship turned from its course and his warriors reached the high world, bends only to give to suppliants and never opens to take; but now, when he came leading the thunangai dance by lamplight, giving his lead hand to others, his queen grew angry, trembling like a sprout in a flood, refused him the small red kuvalai he begged for, asked 'who are you to us?' and turned away with a hot look, so that he who is able at taking the parasol kings' forts is asked how he can be able here.
nuance: The colophon's குரவைநிலை names the dance, and the poem sets a domestic oodal inside a praise of war and giving: the hand that never opens to receive (lines 11, 12) is the hand that begs a flower from the queen and is refused (line 23). The closing lines are hard; they seem to play the king's strength against forts against his helplessness before her.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the hand that wins wars and only gives, then shows the king refused by his queen

comparisons.tenor: the army spreading into foreign land
the queen's small feet, like an opening flower

comparisons.vehicle: ஞாயிற்(று) உருபுகிளர் வண்ணம் கொண்ட வான்தோய் வெண்குடை
comparisons.tenor: the kings' parasols, bright as the sun

reading: The poet tells the king that when the foes he camped against give tribute and he grants them grace and goes home to his ancient famous city, he should take another road and not lead his elephant past the forts his forebears guarded, with their trap-set gates, crocodile moats and sky-high walls, because, apart from the forts he won himself, his spotted-browed elephant, on seeing any gate of gold-bound planks, will brush off the goad, curl its trunk and charge with the banner waving, and none can hold it.
nuance: The praise is a warning against the king's own city: the elephant has broken so many gates that it cannot tell a friendly gate from an enemy's, so the hyperbole flatters the army while seeming to fear it. வேங்கை (line 18) is read as the tiger whose stripes the brow outdoes; it could also be the vengai tree, whose spotted flowers are the usual image.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's war elephant by warning it would charge his own forts

comparisons.tenor: the elephant's spotted brow, outdoing the tiger's

reading: The poet says she came to see the king because people called him a giver, wishes that he achieve what he intends and that his garland live, and since every day he scatters choice vessels without limit to end the suppliants' distress while the bright-jewelled viralis sing his valour, she wishes that he not go to the high world but abide long here on the broad earth, lord of an army that, when the drum sounds and the lancers rise with the young men, will not stand still once it sees the foes' elephants.
nuance: The blessing reverses the usual reward: the giver's merit would carry him to the high world, and the poet asks that he forgo it and stay where the suppliants are (lines 9 to 11). The colophon's காட்சிவாழ்த்து matches the first line: she came because of his name and blesses on seeing him.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet blesses the king on seeing him, drawn by his name as a giver

comparisons.tenor: the viralis' rounded shoulders, like bamboo
the viralis' jewels, bright as lightning

reading: The poet hails the king as husband of the noble queen, protector of the worthy, lord of the cool sea-garden land of fragrant thaazhai shores, shield of the Mazhavar, king of the Kudavar, who even when suppliants do not come sends chariots to bring them and gives them food, and wishes that his days, beyond the measure of years he desires, may go like the white clouds that pour rain, protect the land and rise to rest on the hill, he whose anger cooled only after he took the high-hilled lands of wailing kings.
nuance: The king does not wait to be asked (வாரார் ஆயினும், line 10): he fetches the suppliants. The blessing takes the rain cloud not as the model of giving but of a life that rests after giving, the cloud going up to the hill when its work is done. Lines 7 and 8 (the white pulse mash without red meat, the white meat as provision) read as the food of the Mazhavar warriors, whose shield he is.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king who fetches suppliants and feeds them, and blesses his days

comparisons.tenor: the king's days passing after his giving

reading: The poet says the king is no skilled dancer before the drums of the dancers in the wide festival ground, long live his garland, but when the victory drum sounds, with sword raised, shining ornaments and a golden uzhinai garland, he is the king who dances on the battlefield where the kings who attacked him in their great folly lose their lives.
nuance: A mock dispraise: the denial of skill at the festival sets up the dance that counts, the victory dance with the bright sword that the colophon's ஒள்வாள் அமலை names. The uzhinai garland (line 5) is the siege flower, so the field he dances on is one where he took forts.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victory dance on the field where hostile kings died

reading: The speaker urges the small-bangled virali, walking on soft paths on her small feet, to tune the paalai mode on the bards' great lute, sing the thazhinji, and come with her, for they shall go to see the victorious king who danced the thunangai on the reeking battlefield where blood reddens his anklet and palmyra garland, husband of the restrained and wise queen who bore young sons, who fears the distress of suppliants more than the sulking eyes of bright-browed women and welcomes those who come for his support.
nuance: The opening formula செல்லா மோதில் (line 6) is read here as செல்லாமோ தில், 'shall we not go', the same words that open Purananuru 64. The king's anxiety is ranked: the suppliant's sad face is a greater fear to him than the oodal of the women of his house (lines 13, 14).

thinai_evidence.note: a guide poem sending the virali to the generous king

reading: Let the viralis dance and the gift-seekers sing, says the poet: the great lord of the warriors, who wear kuvalai on white palm leaf and bear sword scars and swore that if they feast today they will not eat tomorrow until they cross the earthen fort wall, the truthful-tongued, fort-breaking archer, shield of the worthy, is called Vaanavaramban, lord of a wide land where on dry ground under the small-leaved velam the farmers yoke their oxen and the ploughshare turns up bright gems.
nuance: The vow (lines 5 to 7) belongs to the warriors, not the king, and binds their next meal to the taking of the wall. The poem ends on a plough that turns up gems in poor dry land, so the warlike king is finally praised as lord of farmers.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king as lord of vow-bound warriors and of a farming land

reading: As in the cold month of Maasi, when the night is long, the sun rises in the east and spreads its rays to end the darkness and gladden the bard crossing the cold wastes, so the king makes the small homes of suppliants grow; the poet asks whether his anger will cool if foes who opposed him without knowing his refuge bow and pay tribute, and tells him that it is his duty too to protect the land where goods of hill and sea are shared out and the roads are kept unblocked in the way of dharma.
nuance: The last lines (16 to 19) turn praise into a statement of duty (கடனே): keeping the roads open so the goods of hill and sea can be exchanged is named as the king's charge, beside his giving. The simile is timed: the sun of the long Maasi night is the one most longed for, as the bard on the cold road longs for the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of the king's giving and a statement of his duty to the land

comparisons.tenor: the king, whose rising makes the suppliants' homes grow

reading: The speaker asks the bard woman whether they shall not go to see the king, whose army is set on killing and who is himself set on war yet gives without ceasing, where sweet fruit that bees swarm over and ripe fruit with honeyed pulp end the weariness of travellers, the harvest never fails, and warriors with unstrung bows live by the sea whose spray mingles with the mist and whose wind brings cold.
nuance: The first line sets the king's killing and his giving side by side without joining them. The last line (துவ்வா நறவின் சாயினத் தானே) may name the place where he stays, perhaps the Chera port Naravu, or speak of toddy; the reading is open.

thinai_evidence.note: a guide poem sending the bard woman to the king who wars and gives

reading: The decade's preface says that Adukotpattu Cheralathan, son of Kudakko Nedunjeralathan by the queen born of the Vel Avi line, brought to Thondi the goats seized in Dandaranya and had them given, gave the Brahmins tawny cows and a village in Kudanadu, made the name Vaanavaramban shine, crushed the other Mazhavar in war, drove off kings, protected his people as one tends an infant, and had a just heart, and that Kakkaipadiniyar Nachchellaiyar sang this ten.
nuance: The preface ties the king's name to a seizure of goats (வருடை, line 3; ஆடு கோள்), while the songs play on ஆடு as dance (52, 56, 57); the two explanations sit side by side in the same decade. The title Vaanavaramban, which 58 gives him in the songs, is here earned by a gift.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's deeds, gifts and protection

comparisons.tenor: the king protecting his people, as nurses tend an infant

title: 7ஆம் பத்து, செல்வக்கடுங்கோ வாழிஆதன்
theme: The seventh ten, Kapilar's songs for Selvakkadungo Vazhiathan: the poet arrives after Pari's death, drawn by a giver who does not regret his gifts; sieges and the terms of surrender, the king defined by four exceptions, gifts to brahmins and musicians that outshine other kings as the sun the stars, two guide songs to bards, warriors fasting before a fort while palace women mark days on the wall, ancestors who ruled like him, and the ancient debts paid; the preface adds his mother's line, his sacrifice and the gift of Okanthur.
source_issues: 61-70: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); the patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
62 and 68 are marked uzhinai and 69 vanji from their content (sieges, the march); the colophons give paadaan thurais, with 69 as வஞ்சித்துறைப் பாடாண்பாட்டு.
68: the colophon writes செந்துறைப்பாடாண்பாட்டு without the space the other colophons have; normalised in puram_thurai.
62 line 3 and 64 line 9 share the line எஃகுபடை அறுத்த கொய்சுவல் புரவி; 62 line 1 and 64 line 10 share இழைஅணிந்(து); not flagged.
65 line 4 repeats 90 line 39 and 66 line 19 repeats 76 line 14, as flagged.
Repaired TSCII leftovers (flags): 62 lines 16 and 18, 63 lines 3 and 8, 64 line 19, 65 line 2, 67 lines 5 and 22, 69 lines 8 and 12, 70 line 23; the repaired readings fit.
61 line 16 (நிலவின்அன்ன வெள்வேல் பாடினி) joins a white spear to the singing woman; the reading is odd and may hide a corruption.
patikam:7 lines 9-10 (ஓத்திர நெல்லின் ஒகந்தூர் ஈத்துப் புரோசு மயக்கி) are obscure; line 13 (கபிலர் பாடினார் பத்துப்பாட்டு.) is the prose colophon kept as a verse line.

reading: Kapilar tells the Chera, lord of a land where the north wind carries the smell of toddy from ripe jackfruit and husband of a woman like a painted doll in a house like a painting, that since Pari of the broad chest, whose giving never dried though his sandal paste did, has gone to the far land from which no one returns, so that the drums' clay has dried and suppliants grieve, he has not come begging nor will he say less than the truth: what drew him was the king's fame, which says he does not regret what he gave nor exult each time he gives, and so he has come to the camp, rank with the flesh of strong elephants, where the singing woman's clapping hands stand in for the drum, to share a joy like a festival.
nuance: The poem opens the decade with Kapilar's own history: Pari is dead (line 10, வாராச் சேண்புலம் படர்ந்தோன்), and the new patron is measured by a formula of giving without regret or elation (lines 12-13) that sounds like Pari's. Calling the Chera the enemy of the unnam (line 6), the omen tree, makes him a king who does not wait on signs. Line 11 is the bard's own ethic: he will neither beg nor trim his words.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's giving, which drew him after his patron's death

comparisons.tenor: the singing woman's clapping hands, which take the drum's place
the king's joyous drinking in camp

reading: The poet tells the victorious king, fierce as a lion, whose ornamented elephants, shields many as clouds and horses with cropped manes surround strong forts and whose fire falls on them as if suns had multiplied, that if his enemies behind moats and hill-like walls name their goads and bow and pay tribute, then their broad land will remain one fit for song, with cattle spread over grassy fields, heaps of threshed grain piled by the kaanji trees, and strong-handed toddy-drinking workers, crowned with stream lilies, waving off the striped bees.
nuance: The fertile farm scene of lines 13-19 is not description of the king's own land but the reward held out to an enemy who submits; the poem stops before saying what happens otherwise, and the siege of lines 1-7 has already said it.

thinai_evidence.note: the king besieges forts and offers the besieged a choice between tribute and ruin

comparisons.tenor: the bright fire that falls on the besieged fort

reading: The poet tells the Chera that he bows only to brahmins, his eyes are shy only before friends, his fragrant chest scarred by the bow opens only to women, and his spoken word will not fail even if the earth changes its nature; wearing the small-leaved uzhinai garland, crushing the Tamil foes with plunder and raging like thunder that shakes hills, he drove off two kings in one siege, so that the defeated warriors said they had seen his like, and since he won even with their own yoke, the poet wishes the lord of the Cheras, if any good has been done in this sea-girt world, a life of countless ages.
nuance: Four lines end alike (அல்லது ... அறியலையே): the poem defines the king by his four exceptions, so his pride, fear, love and truth each have one bounded outlet. The uzhinai garland of line 8 marks the deed as a siege.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's character and wishes him long life

comparisons.tenor: the king raging against the foe

reading: Many kings have drums of victory and true swords, says the poet, but this one, after a renowned sacrifice whose brahmins with tongues that proclaim dharma took rare vessels, has a fixed rule that when he sees musicians at the guarded gate of his sandy courtyard, where elephants wallowed in the mud of poured water, he says at once 'give them horses with cropped manes, swaying chariots and jewels'; so, as the rising sun puts out the many stars, the poet has come to praise the strong foot that broke his foes, a lord who, with the look of neythal blooming in the dark backwater, pours more benefit than the high cloud and has ended the hunger of the hungry kin.
nuance: The sun-and-stars simile answers lines 1-2: other kings also have drums and swords, so what makes this one the sun is the gift at the gate, not the war. The giving begins at a sacrifice, to brahmins, and passes at once to musicians.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's giving to brahmins and musicians

comparisons.tenor: the king outshining the many other kings

reading: The poet hails the king as chief of warriors worthy of kaanchi, whose plumed horses have hooves red from trampling corpses, wealth of those who shelter behind the bowmen's guard, husband of the red-jewelled lady whose breasts, waist, wide eyes, bamboo-like shoulders and fragrant brow are joined to a chastity that rules even the god of desire, protector of bards and treasure of gift-seekers, and says that he has happily seen the king's daily feasting assembly, where, as a master of the paalai mode on the sweet strings changes the mournful tune, the king's toddy-joy, rich in festival wealth, gives like a rain that changes things.
nuance: The lute simile is exact about music: the master shifts the mournful (பையுள்) mode, so the king's gift is pictured as a change of key in the suppliant's life, not merely a quantity. Line 4 recurs at 90 line 39.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet praises the king's daily feast and giving

comparisons.vehicle: பாலை வல்லோன் பையுள் உறுப்பின் பண்ணுப் பெயர்த்தாங்குச்
comparisons.tenor: the king's feast turning gift-seekers' sorrow into joy

reading: The poet tells an old-tongued bard who goes playing the paalai mode on his great lute with its curved neck that the king, who vowed with his thundering drum and crushed the massed spears of his foes in a corpse-strewn field, gives, they say, plentiful food, elephants brought as old tribute and paddy measured in heaps, a leader like peaks clouded with morning rain who bore the enemy's onslaught, lord of a wide land where in the festival of swords warriors wear palm leaf strung with the god's tufted vaakai flower, birds, looking like those flowers, roost in the pidavu clusters by the flowering mullai of the forest, and bright gems are found in the red gravel mixed with crystal.
nuance: The poem is a guide song in all but its colophon: it addresses the bard and promises food. Its landscape image folds war into land: the vaakai flower worn for victory is the vehicle for ordinary birds in a mullai thicket, so the king's country itself wears his victory flower.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet directs a bard to the king's giving

comparisons.tenor: the king who bore the enemy's charge
the gleaming spears raised above the shields
the birds roosting round the mullai and pidavu

reading: The poet tells a skilled bard of the old city of Panthar, with his famed kin of Kodumanam, that he will receive sea pearls and fine jewels if he goes singing to the wealthy lord of high stony Neri, where the bee, sucking the open kaanthal without pause, loses its hum in dread of the hill's spirit; that lord of warriors who wear konrai garlands with white palm strips and bodies scarred by swords, hacked like the butchers' chopping block on which they cut great curved-horned bulls, has made the land tremble in many battles, with banners waving, horns and conches roaring, elephant herds moving, vultures drinking blood on fields spread with fat, headless trunks standing like sacrificial posts and the formless demon woman stirring dread.
nuance: The promised gifts name their sources: Kodumanam and Panthar were known for beads and pearls, so the bard's home towns are themselves the treasure. The bee on Neri that cannot hum for dread is a quiet echo of the battlefield's terror, set in the king's own hill.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet guides a bard to the king

comparisons.tenor: the headless trunks standing on the field

reading: In the camp pitched in a foreign land, where the drum beaten with fierce sticks roars through the sky like the sea with the wind for its drumstick, the king's men, who will not eat until they have stormed the fort, pass many days eager at heart and weary in body, and wonder whether, once they have taken the enemy's dwelling, they will carry off the white tusks of his riding elephants, pay with them in the market of fluttering toddy flags, and, more content than the nameless untroubled dwellers of the northern land, have many sweet delights each day; meanwhile, in the long-walled palace, sleepless women whose green jewels slip draw the passing days on the painted walls until their red fingers redden, women bound by the king's fragrant chest.
nuance: The poem holds two waits side by side: the warriors fasting until the fort falls and the women marking days on the wall. The akam figure of the woman counting days (compare Kural 1261) is set inside a war poem, where it measures the length of the siege. Who the wall-marking women are, the king's or the warriors', is not said; line 19 binds them to the king's chest.

thinai_evidence.note: the warriors have vowed not to eat until the fort falls

comparisons.tenor: the war drum thundering in the camp
the warriors' hoped-for life of delight

reading: The poet tells the victorious king, whose sky-touching banners on mountain-like elephants wave like waterfalls on peaks, whose drum roars like the wind-struck sea before an army like the sea, and who with broken swords, chosen spears, tested horses and eager warriors heaped corpses and made his enemies' families wander ruined, that those who rolled the bright wheel of rule before him surely ruled this earth because, like him, they were of unwavering purpose, and in their time the land poured its yield, the sun's heat softened, Venus stood in its good place, the sky widened and the rains answered the people's need, and the four quarters prospered together.
nuance: The comparison runs backwards: the ancestors are said to be like the present king (நின்போல், line 11), so he is the standard and they the copies. The good signs of lines 13-17 (the earth's yield, the gentle sun, Venus in place, timely rain) are the marks of rule that the second decade gives to the present king's land.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's army marches on and ruins the enemy

comparisons.tenor: the banners waving on the elephants

reading: The poet hails the king whose feet drove elephants, whose arrows harmed horses, whose spear crowded the battle and whose shoulders and strong hand bent the bow, who wears the palmyra's white leaf that bees do not hum over and flowers of sweet springs, defeated kings and destroyed their pride, husband of a lady of chastity who is true even in jest and never hears slander, and says that with his unfailing kin around him he fed the gods with sacrifice, pleased the sages with learning, bent in gentleness but never in manhood, cared for elders more than for his young sons and paid the ancient debts, and wishes his days to be unending like high Ayirai, whose falls drop with a drum's voice heard even by the dwellers of heaven.
nuance: Lines 17-22 list what the king owes and has paid: gods by sacrifice (வேள்வியின்), sages by learning (கேள்வி), and elders before sons; தொல்கடன் names it as an inherited debt, not a virtue. Line 20 (வணங்கிய சாயல் வணங்கா ஆண்மை) puts the decade's balance in one line.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises the king's conquests and duties and wishes him long life

reading: The decade's preface says that Selvakkadungo Vazhiathan, son of Porayan's queen, who was the daughter of Anthuvan of unflagging heart and long, subtle learning who bound his foes, settled lands, drove off enemies, won many battles with a dreaded army, performed a praised and ample sacrifice, went the way of dharma, held Mayavannan in his heart, gave Okanthur with its paddy and outdid the priests, and shone spotless with a generous mind; and that Kapilar sang this ten.
nuance: The preface names a gift the songs do not: a village, Okanthur, given after the sacrifice. Its devotion to Mayavannan sits beside the brahmin-facing duties of 63, 64 and 70.

thinai_evidence.note: the preface praises the king's lineage, wars, sacrifice and gifts

title: 8ஆம் பத்து, பெருஞ்சேரல் இரும்பொறை
theme: The eighth ten, Arisil Kizhar's songs for Perunjeral Irumporai: foes who stirred the hive and paid tribute, the doom-fire for those who resolve without thought, a king beyond comparison whom praise cannot make credible, a learned sacrificer who sends his old counsellor to tapas, an army too large to count, a virali sent to the hill of the destroyer of Tagadur, a couch made of a beaten king's tusks; the preface names Adhiyaman and the razing of Tagadur.
source_issues: 71-80: no poem colophon gives a thinai (all null); eight thurais are paadaan forms, 77 is உழிஞை அரவம் and 78 விறலியாற்றுப்படை. The patikam has neither thinai nor thurai.
