reading: I will no longer long for the three kings of the sea-bounded land with their roaring drums and herds of elephants; you are the one I know: in your land seed sown in the crowded pond does not die in drought but thrives like cane, flowers like eyes bloom even when summer dries the rain-water, and water like sapphire flows to the sea carrying the gold-like petals of the dark-stemmed vengai; lord of Nanjil of the red hills, ruler of the land of great rocks and small white falls, long may you live, and long live the father and mother who bore you.
nuance: The poet's renunciation of the three crowned kings is the measure of the small chief: a land that never fails in drought is a patron who never fails a bard. The blessing on the parents is a closing formula of praise.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief and his fertile land

comparisons.tenor: the seed that thrives in drought

reading: Bard in rags, with your small lute of strong-voiced strings, who crossed many paths full of cattle, left behind hills full of deer and swam many fords full of fish to come here: do not worry; your lord will never say 'come back later', for the husband of the lady with thick dark hair is like the great ear of grain in the wide field the parrots frequent, so who would know beforehand that you were coming?
nuance: The image of the grain-ear the parrots feed on makes the patron a crop open to any bird that comes, so no appointment is needed. The poem names no patron; the colophon gives Ay.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard directing another bard to a patron

comparisons.vehicle: கிளி மரீஇய வியன் புனத்து மரன் அணி பெருங்குரல்
comparisons.tenor: the patron, open to all who come

reading: Young men with loads pressing their shoulders and dancers with slim waists whose feet ache from the long climb are with me, and to live I speak the truth, not lies: lord of Nanjil of the high peaks, the plough-hill no one ploughs, descendant of men who never turned back, this is no time to wait for the ripe moment; the king has not stopped giving, and you do not fear death for your king, so if one day a hard battle comes like the earth heaving up, my suffering troupe may come to grief.
nuance: The bard's argument for speed is the patron's courage: a man who will die for his king may not be there tomorrow. The pun of the unploughed plough (உழாஅ நாஞ்சில்) praises the hill and its lord in one phrase.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard urging a patron to give now

reading: The lord of Nanjil with its wide-spreading jackfruit trees is surely a simpleton, red-tongued poets: when we asked for a little rice to go with the greens our bangled dancers had picked in the garden, he, knowing other kinds of due measure, weighed his own standing too and gave us a great elephant like a hill ringed by forest; is there any giving as unknowing as this? Do the great not keep watch over their own duty?
nuance: Praise disguised as blame: the patron is called foolish because he measured the gift by his own greatness rather than by the request. The closing question can be read as mock reproach (the great do not count the cost of their duty) or as a real one.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through a gift far beyond the request

title: புறநானூறு 141-160
theme: Gift poems to the hill chieftains Pekan, Nalli, Ori, the lord of Konkanam, Erai and Kumanan: the guide poems, the cycle pleading with Pekan to return to his wife, the roll of seven dead givers, and the bard's starving household pressed on Kumanan.
source_issues: 141: the colophon thurai reads பாணாற்று படை, without the doubled ப் of பாணாற்றுப்படை (as in 155); name normalised in puram_thurai.

142: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; our line 1 (அறுகுளத்து உகுத்தும், அகல்வயல் பொழிந்தும்) is the first of the three places the rain falls and the simile needs it, so it is marked as part of the poem.

143 to 147: these are puram poems on akam matter (a patron's neglected wife), marked akam_puram mixed with thinai perunthinai, as their colophons have it; the bard who pleads is coded as paanan speaking to the thalaivan.
147: line 5 is flagged as repeated in 349 line 5 (a formula for a woman's eyes); line 6 has an edition variant noted in the flags, our reading kept.
148 line 3: கனிற்றொடு looks like a misprint for களிற்றொடு (with elephants); marked as elephant.
149: the colophon thurai is பரிசில், but the poem asks for nothing and states the effect of Nalli's giving, which fits இயன்மொழி (the review notes the site's Iyan Mozhi); colophon kept as is.
152 line 20: ழுறையுளிக் is a misprint for முறையுளிக் (in due order).
152 and 153: the colophon poet is spelt வண்பரணர், and 148 to 150 have வன்பரணர் / வன் பரணர்; likely one poet, spelt two ways.
154 line 13: கொண்டுபெருங்கானம் is very likely a misprint for கொண்பெருங்கானம், the name in 156 line 2.

155 line 7: கொண்பெருங்காலத்துக் is very likely a misprint for கொண்பெருங்கானத்துக் (the patron's land, as in 156); so no place entity is recorded for 155. Line 2 closes its quotation with ” after opening with ‘.
159 line 5: முதுர்வினள் looks like a misprint for முதிர்வினள் (aged).

160: the flags give four misprint candidates (line 6 குனிப்ப/குளிப்ப, line 10 கோடின்றாக/கேடின்றாக, line 14 நல்குவை/நல்குவன், line 21 வருங்கலம்/வறுங்கலம்); the reading follows the editions' வறுங்கலம் (empty pots) at line 21, and the review says our text lacks two lines of the site's (its 8 and 17). Marked uncertain; not compared against the site.

tamil: படா அம் மஞ்ஞைக்கு ஈத்த எம் கோ,
reading: A bard resting on the road with his chariot unyoked, wearing a gold lotus and with his viṟali garlanded, answers a hungry bard who keeps asking who they are: before they saw Pekan they were poorer than he is, for Pekan, who gave a cloak to a peacock knowing it could neither wear nor wrap it, gives not with an eye to the next world but with an eye to other people's want.
nuance: The cloak given to a peacock is offered as proof of motive: a gift to a creature that can neither use it nor repay it cannot be a bid for merit, so Pekan's famous folly becomes the evidence that he looks only at others' need (வறுமை நோக்கின்று), not at the next world (மறுமை). The guide also admits that he was once poorer than the man he guides (நின்னினும் புல்லியேம்).

thinai_evidence.note: a guide's praise of a patron's giving, which is paadaan

comparisons.tenor: the rewarded bards resting at ease in the wild tract

reading: Like the rain that by its unbounded habit pours into the drained tank, over the broad field, and wastes itself on salt land where it helps no one, Pekan of the rutting elephant and warrior's anklet is foolish only in giving, never foolish in battle when other armies come at him.
nuance: கொடைமடம், folly in giving, is a fault named as praise: the poet concedes that Pekan gives without discrimination, as rain falls on salt land, then pairs it with the folly he lacks (படைமடம்), so the one fault becomes the measure of his greatness in the other field.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's giving and valour

comparisons.tenor: Pekan's giving, which falls on the deserving and undeserving alike

reading: Kapilar addresses Pekan, lord of a hill where the Kuravar, having made offerings to the god about the rain and rejoicing that it turned as they asked, eat their millet, and asks who that pitiable woman was who yesterday, in a small village by the waterfalls, when his hungry troupe stood at her door praising Pekan and his hill, could not stop her tears and wept aloud, wetting her breast, like a lamenting flute.
nuance: The poet never says the woman is Pekan's wife: the question யார்கொல் அளியள் leaves him to supply the answer, and it is the song in his praise that makes her weep, so the praise poem turns into the reproach. The hill people whose prayer was answered stand at the opening against a woman whose waiting is not.

thinai_evidence.note: a woman's weeping for an absent husband told to the man himself, which is the unmatched love of perunthinai

tamil: கலுழ்ந்து, வார் அரிப் பனி பூண்அகம் நனைப்ப,
reading: Paranar tells Pekan that his want of pity is cruel: when the bards at nightfall played the sevvazhi mode and sang of his forest that meets the rains, a woman whose kohl-lined eyes outshone the neythal flower wept until her tears wet her ornaments, and when they bowed and asked whether she was kin to their patron she wiped her eyes with fingers like kaanthal buds and said she was not, only that he is said to drive there always in his loud chariot, desiring the beauty of a woman like her, to the good town fenced with mullai.
nuance: Asked whether she is his kin, she denies being his kin and names the other woman only as one 'like me', so the wife's restraint carries the rebuke the poet does not make himself. The cycle 143 to 147 shows several poets taking up one patron's domestic breach in turn.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife weeping for a husband who goes to another woman, told to him by the bards

comparisons.tenor: her kohl-lined eyes, more beautiful than the flower

reading: Paranar reminds Pekan, famed for giving a cloak to the peacock in pity lest it shiver, that the bards come neither from hunger nor with a burden to lay down: the gift they beg, playing the small lute until listeners tremble and crying 'do this dharma, lover of grace', is that he mount his chariot tonight and end the grief of the woman who lives in sorrow.
nuance: The peacock is turned against Pekan: if he pitied a bird that might be cold, he cannot leave a woman in sorrow. By declaring that they are not hungry, the bards empty the parisil form of its usual content and make it a plea for reconciliation.

thinai_evidence.note: the wife abiding in grief for an absent husband, which the bards plead for

comparisons.tenor: the dark stem of the small lute

reading: Arisil Kizhar tells Pekan to keep his rare jewels and wealth: if, after the bard has sung his good hard-soiled land in the sevvazhi mode, he wishes to give a gift, let it be that his wife, who wastes away in grief at his neglect, may perfume her soft hair, thick as a peacock's gathered tail, with fragrant smoke and wear a cool garland, and that his horses be yoked to his tall chariot.
nuance: The gift is described entirely through the wife's toilet: the incense and the garland she has given up will come back when he does, so the poem asks for his return without stating it, and ends by commanding his horses rather than him.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife enduring her husband's neglect, the gift asked being his return

reading: Perunkunrur Kizhar tells the lord of the Aviyar that he has crossed many hills of cave-fed falls playing the sevvazhi mode, and that the gift he asks is this: that the lovely woman with streaked, rain-dark eyes, who heard alone yesterday the sweet rumble of the dark clouds and lives in one corner in loneliness, should wash clean as an earth-dulled gem her dark hair left without oil and crowd it with fresh flowers, if he goes back today.
nuance: The rain-cloud heard 'yesterday' is the season of promised return, so the gift is set against a deadline already passed; hair left without oil (நெய்யொடு துறந்த) is the sign of a wife who has given up adornment while she waits, and the poet asks for it to be reversed today.

thinai_evidence.note: a wife living alone through the rains her husband was to return by

comparisons.tenor: her hair washed clean of its neglect

reading: Nalli of the high hill loud with falls: having praised his tireless strength and the wealth people long for, the poet has been given daily, in his bright great house, fine jewels with elephants, gifts in full, so that his small red tongue no longer knows how to recite deeds never done in seeking praise from kings without merit.
nuance: The poem praises by renouncing a genre: Nalli's gifts have made flattery unnecessary, so the poet's honesty is counted among the things Nalli gave him. It also admits that bards did invent deeds for meaner patrons.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron's giving through its effect on the poet's speech

reading: Long live Nalli: because of the generosity with which he has taken on the duty of keeping them, the poet's people have forgotten the order of their modes, playing marutham in the hushed evening and sevvazhi in the morning.
nuance: The praise is a joke against the bards: plenty has done what hunger never did and made them lose the clock of their own craft, since each mode had its hour. The poem asks for nothing, which is why the colophon's பரிசில் sits awkwardly on it.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through what his giving has done to the bards

reading: In a cloak torn like an autumn kite's dark wing, the poet lay at the foot of a jack tree, past caring for himself, when a strong-bowed hunter with a gem on his head and an anklet bloody from killing deer saw his weariness, made him sit as he rose to bow, roasted white fat on a fire he struck himself before his men caught up, and bade him eat with his kin; when the poet had eaten, drunk at the cool falls and made to leave, the hunter said a forest people have no other rare treasure and gave him the chain from his chest and the bracelet from his arm, told neither his country nor his name, and only from others did the poet learn that he was Nalli, lord of the hill guarded by Thotti.
nuance: The poem turns on what Nalli withholds, his country and his name, so the gift comes without the fame it usually buys, and the poet repays him by naming him in the last line. He cooks with his own fire before his attendants arrive. Line 25 plays on தோட்டி, an elephant goad and the name of the hill: a goad 'not forged of iron'.

thinai_evidence.note: a patron's giving told as an encounter, plain praise

comparisons.tenor: the white fat of the kill
the sweet water of the hill

reading: The poet tells the young Vicchi lord why he embraced Kandeerakkon and not him: Kandeerakkon is of a house so generous that when the lord of the sky-touching hill is away even its women give jewelled young she-elephants to delight singers as of old; the Vicchi lord, kin of Nannan of the golden chariot, would also have deserved an embrace, but because of a door shut against singers the poet's people have shunned his fragrant great hill where the clouds pour.
nuance: An embrace was a public honour that a poet could give or withhold, and this poem justifies a public snub. Whose door was shut, the young lord's or his line's, is not certain from the text. The irrealis மன்னே ('you would have been fit') keeps the refusal courteous.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of one patron set against blame of another

tamil: வேட்டுவர் இல்லை, நின் ஒப் போர்’ என,
தான் உயிர் செகுத்த மான் நிணப் புழுக்கோடு,
reading: The poet tells how he met a hunter whose one arrow felled an elephant, passed through a gape-mouthed tiger, rolled a spotted stag, dropped a boar and lodged in an iguana in an anthill; guessing that this rich killer, plainly no man who sells, might be Ori, lord of the fruitful hill, he had his viṟali and troupe set up drum, lute, horn and pipes and played all twenty-one modes in order, and when they hailed him as 'king' the man was abashed because it was his own name and, not letting them go, gave them the meat of his kill, toddy like melted ghee and gold and gems from his hill, there in the wilderness: the lord of tall Kolli, eager for unguarded giving.
nuance: The single arrow through five beasts is the poem's credential for the man before he is named, and the bards test their guess by performance: hailed as கோ, he is abashed because it is his own name. As in 150, the patron is met as a hunter in the forest, not at court.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's giving and the bard's dismissal with gifts

comparisons.tenor: the hunter, who does not look like one who sells his kill

reading: The poet's troupe of performers went to see the rain-like giving of Athan Ori, lord of the cloud-clad hill who daily gives jewelled elephants to suppliants, and received garlands of gold lilies on white fibre that no cold water ever bloomed, ornaments and herds of elephants; now, perhaps because they are no longer hungry, they will neither dance nor sing to their tight-strung drums.
nuance: The lilies 'that do not bloom in cold water' are gold work, so even the flowers are imperishable; and the closing joke, that the troupe stopped performing when it stopped being hungry, admits that the bards' art ran on need.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through the wealth of his bards

reading: Even beside the wave-beaten sea people ask someone they know for a little water to quench their thirst, and so poets, though they live among kings, go to the faultlessly generous; the poet therefore does not ask what he will get, but came because he thought of the patron: to say 'give' is hard, but whether he gives or not, singing his valour that does not run from thrown spears and his great forest of Konkanam, where cool falls come down like spread white cloth, is easy.
nuance: Kings are the sea, vast and undrinkable; the generous small lord is the little sweet water got from someone known. The poet separates what parisil poems usually join: asking is hard for him, praising is easy, so the praise is offered as free.

thinai_evidence.note: the poet's approach to a patron for a gift, parisil under paadaan

comparisons.tenor: poets who live among kings but go to the generous
the falls of the patron's forest

reading: Bard who hug the small curved-stemmed lute to your wasted side and cry out for someone to understand and end your distress, listen: as the pale white flower of the nerunchi in a deserted village opens to face the rising sun, the bowls of needy poets open in bloom when they face the cool-garlanded chest of the lord of Konperunkanam of shining fame.
nuance: The image is a weed of the deserted village that turns to the sun, so the poor are flowers of a ruined place and the patron is their sun; the flower's colour is பசலை, the word akam keeps for the pallor of lovesickness.

thinai_evidence.note: one bard directing another to a patron, aatruppadai under paadaan

comparisons.vehicle: நெருஞ்சிப் பசலை வான்பூ ஏர்தரு சுடரின் எதிர்கொண்டு
comparisons.tenor: the poor poets' bowls opening toward the patron

reading: Other hills have one good thing, but Konperunkanam always has two: it will lie open for the suppliants who come to it in desire to gather and eat, and besides that it has the lord who sends kings with numberless armies home after taking their tribute.
nuance: The poem counts a hill's goods like assets: the land itself feeds suppliants, and the lord feeds it with kings' tribute, so giving and conquest are two products of one place.

thinai_evidence.note: plain praise of a patron's land and conquest

reading: Bearing with the faults of one's own kin, feeling shame at others' destitution, having a strength that never brings disgrace on the army, and walking tall in the assembly of kings are not fitting for your lords; they fit our Erai, chief of the Kuravar, with broad chest, killing spear and kodal chaplet, lord of the great hill on whose cloud-cleared heights, at dusk, a fine stag that has lost its herd and cannot find its lair calls to its young doe while the spotted tiger in the rock cave listens.
nuance: The virtues are those the Kural later files under shame and forbearance, claimed here by a woman poet of the Kuravar for her own hill chief against other men's lords. Who நும்மோர் ('your people') are is not certain. The closing scene of the stag, the doe and the listening tiger is left without comment.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a hill chief's virtues

reading: Now that the seven are dead who fought and gave, Pari of Parambu, Ori who ruled Kolli, Malaiyan who rode Kari to victory, Ezhini of the horse held but not ridden, Pekan of the great hill guarded by a god, Ay whom Mosi sang, and Nalli who drove off his foes and gave without refusing, the poet has hurried here thinking of Kumanan to end the need of suppliants, and blesses the lord of Muthiram, where a male monkey that has eaten an old thorny jackfruit calls his soft-headed mate with his hand, that his spear may prevail over his enemies along with his famed generosity.
nuance: The roll of seven makes generosity a line of succession with a gap that Kumanan is invited to fill, so the praise is also a summons. Each giver gets one emblem, compressing whole poems into an epithet. 'The horse held but not ridden' (ஊராது ஏந்திய குதிரை) may be Ezhini's hill named Kuthirai; the text does not settle it.

thinai_evidence.note: a blessing on a patron, with a plea for gifts

tamil: தீர்தல்செல் லாது, என் உயிர்’ எனப் பலபுலந்து,
reading: The poet's mother, so old she complains that her life will not leave her, walks in short steps on a stick, hair like spread thread, never past the yard; his wife, pale and worn, her breasts dried by the many small children who knead and suck them, boils without salt the unripe shoots of rubbish-heap greens, forgets rice, eats the greens without buttermilk and, in soiled scant cloth, goes without and does not blame virtue; so that both their hearts and his hungry kin may rejoice, as cloud pours on a hunters' burnt clearing whose millet would not ear, he will not take a gift given grudgingly though it were a tusked killer elephant, but given gladly he will take even a kunri seed's worth, and asks Kumanan to grant it so.
nuance: After the longest picture of household hunger in the chapter, the demand is about manner, not size: an elephant given grudgingly is refused and a kunri seed given gladly accepted, so the bard puts the giver's gladness above his family's need. அறம் பழியா, his wife does not blame virtue though she starves, gives the household its own pride.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a gift, parisil kadaanilai

comparisons.tenor: the patron's gift reviving the starving household

tamil: இல் உணாத் துறத்தலின், இல் மறந்து உறையும்
reading: Told by Kumanan's praisers that this lord of Muthiram, who flings away hard-won gold vessels so that the bards' troupe may not fail, would revive him like rain on a sun-scorched forest with rich seasoned rice and ghee served in small gold dishes ringed like stars around the moon, the poet hurried, driven by his heart, from a house where his little tufted son sucks his mother's milkless breast and cries opening the empty pots, while she quiets him with the tiger and the moon and at last asks him to show how he sulks when he thinks of his father; and he asks to be sent off quickly with lasting wealth so that she who suffers in waking life may flourish, and will praise Kumanan's fame across the sea-girt earth.
nuance: Lines 1 to 14 quote the hearsay that brought him, so the poem holds Kumanan to a reputation. The mother uses the tiger and the moon, the props of nursery talk, in place of food. Four lines are flagged as possible misprints and the review finds two lines missing, so details of the household scene are not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a quick gift

comparisons.vehicle: முளிபுல் கானம் குழைப்பக், கல்லென அதிர்குரல் ஏறோடு துளிசொரிந் தாங்கு
comparisons.tenor: Kumanan's food reviving a starving body
the small gold dishes ringed around the rice

title: புறநானூறு 161-180
theme: Poems 161-180 are almost all about giving and asking: Perunchiththiranar's and Saththanar's pleas to Kumanan and his gift of his own head, a bard's elephant tied in rebuke to a mean patron's tree, the hill chief Pittankotran praised by five poets as giver and as an anvil to his foes, the hunger-healer Pannan, and soldiers and small chiefs whose scars and spears feed the bards, with one brahmin sacrificer praised as a patron.
source_issues: 166: the colophon thurai reads பார்பபன வாகை, a misprint for பார்ப்பன வாகை; copied exactly in colophon and colophon_form, corrected in puram_thurai name.
172 line 5: வெண்டா looks like a misprint for வேண்டா (do not need to); the sense requires the negative.

171 line 13: உற்றாக reads as a wish that the thorn hurt the patron's foot, which contradicts the blessing; the sense needs a negative wish (as if உறாஅற்க), so the line looks corrupt. Marked uncertain.
162 line 5: கடுமரம் is read as கடிமரம், the guarded tree of a chief's town; the spelling may be a variant or a misprint.
163: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our line 1; line 1 begins the list of those to be given to and is needed by the syntax, so all nine lines are marked.
178: the colophon patron field carries a variant-reading note (பாண்டிக் குதிரைச் சாக்கையன் எனவும் பாடம்) after the name; 179's poet field likewise carries two variant names.
173 line 12 ends with a comma where the poem ends (எமக்கே,).

reading: Perunchiththiranar tells Kumanan, who is a height for him and for others as the clouds that gather from the sea fill the Ganga in the hot season, that his wife, sure he has died on the robber-haunted waste a year ago, should be dazed by the wealth of Kumanan's feet, so he asks to ride home on a tall tusked elephant with face-plate and bells, making kings ashamed, and asks Kumanan to measure him by his own greatness rather than by the bard's skill.
nuance: The wife's lament is quoted inside the petition (lines 9 to 12): the size of the gift is set by her belief that he is dead. What he asks for is a spectacle, an elephant to ride home on so that ungiving kings are shamed, and the closing turn (do not measure me, measure yourself) puts the burden of worth on the giver.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard driven by want asks a chief for a gift

comparisons.tenor: Kumanan as the height that fills bards and others, as cloud-rain fills the Ganga in the hot season
the strong tusker he asks for

reading: Perunchiththiranar tells Ilaveliman that he is not the only patron of suppliants and that patrons are not lacking to them: let him see that askers exist and givers exist; the tall elephant the poet has tied to the guard tree of Ilaveliman's own town, straining it, is the poet's gift, and he is leaving.
nuance: Tying an elephant to a chief's guard tree is what a conqueror does to an enemy; the bard does it with an elephant got elsewhere, so the leave-taking is a rebuke. The colophon's other poems by the same poet suggest the elephant was Kumanan's gift, but this poem does not say whose it was.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard takes leave of a patron over the gift

tamil: நின் நயந்து உறைநர்க்கும், நீ நயந்து உறைநர்க்கும்,
reading: The poet tells his wife to give the wealth that Kumanan of the sharp spear, lord of Muthiram where fruit hangs heavy, has granted to everyone, to those who love her and those she loves, to her kin of manifold virtue and to those who lent to ease the family's hunger, without asking whom to favour, without consulting him and without thinking of saving to live well.
nuance: The gift begged for the starving household is turned out of the house at once: the bard's wife becomes a giver in her own right, and the poem ends by naming the patron, so the redistribution itself is the praise. நெடுங்குறி எதிர்ப்பை (line 4) seems to mean a loan given on a long promise of return; யாழ in line 3 is a particle, not the lute.

thinai_evidence.note: the patron's gift is named and praised through its giving away

reading: Perunthalai Saththanar tells Kumanan that, seeing his hearth so long unused that mushrooms bloom in it, his son crying at each suck of a breast shrivelled and dry from hunger, and his wife's rain-dark eyes brimming, he has come to him, and that now Kumanan knows his state he will not rest without pressing his claim on him, born of a clan that ends the want of drummers and lute players.
nuance: The petition is made of the body: the cold hearth, the dry breast with its closed ducts, the wife's tears. The last lines ground the claim not on Kumanan's mood but on his lineage, which is bound to end the want of performers, so the bard asks as of right and says he will hold the patron to it.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard presses a patron for a gift

reading: Those who wished to last in an unlasting world set up their fame and died, and the very rich who give nothing to the needy are not remembered like the men of old; the poet sang a lord whose elephants never failed singers, and he, saying that a singer going home empty would grieve him more than the loss of his country, gave the poet his sword so that he might take his head, having nothing dearer than himself; with that triumph the poet now comes, having seen the addressee's kinsman of unretreating resolve.
nuance: The argument runs from a maxim (only fame lasts) through its negative (the ungiving rich are forgotten) to the extreme case, a giver who has lost his land and offers his own head. The closing joy is addressed to the giver's kinsman, for whom that head has a price; the poem names neither man, and the story that the kinsman is the brother who drove Kumanan out comes from the colophon tradition, not the verse.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard reports the gift he received

reading: Avur Mulankizhar praises Vinnanthayan, descendant of learned men who, keeping to the word of the ancient matted-haired First One, mastered the one old book of four parts and six limbs, broke the pride of disputants by telling false that looks true from truth, and completed the twenty-one sacrifices; wearing the black-buck skin for the rite, with his wives of chaste conduct doing their parts, he has poured ghee more than water, made sacrifices past counting and spread his fame wider than the earth; the poet wishes always to see him so, receiving guests, and says he will go home to his town on the Kaveri to eat and enjoy, while the brahmin should stand on earth like the bamboo-grown Himalaya.
nuance: The victory in this vaakai is not in war: it lies in debate and in the count of sacrifices, and the poem counts in riddles (one aim, four, six, three times seven). The bard's closing wish to go home and eat makes the sacrificer a patron like any chief. Several phrases (அறம் புகழ்ந்த வலை சூடி, துணைத் துணைவியர்) are obscure to me.

thinai_evidence.note: the brahmin's excellence in learning and sacrifice is the deed praised

comparisons.tenor: the disputants' false arguments that look like truth
the brahmin, wished to stand long and firm on earth

reading: The poet tells Killi of the swift horse that, since he stands against the enemy's army and wins, his sword-scarred body is sweet to hear of and harsh to see, while his enemies, who turn their backs at the sight of him, have unhurt bodies sweet to see and harsh to hear of; each is sweet in one way, so what is there to marvel at in him that the world marvels so?
nuance: The praise is a riddle in the senses: the king's wounds belong to the ear (fame), the enemies' whole skins to the eye, and the closing question pretends there is nothing to wonder at when the whole poem has just said what it is.

thinai_evidence.note: the king's victories and wounds are the deed praised

reading: On the slopes of Kotran's hill, where boars dig up kanthal tubers and the kuravar sow millet in the turned earth without ploughing, then cook the first new grain with wild-cow milk and venison in an unwashed pot over sandalwood and share it on banana leaves in yards fragrant with wild jasmine, the bards, it is said, praise this lord of the unridden horse, chief of bowmen with vengai garlands and generous hands, every day across the Tamil land, so that his unfading fame shames kings who do not give.
nuance: The long kurinji scene praises before the chief is named: a land that feeds without the plough and a meal shared on leaves are the image of his giving. ஊராக் குதிரை, the horse no one rides, reads as the name of his hill (Kuthirai), a riddle on his title.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a giver's fame among bards

reading: Since, when your army advances, you are in its van, and when the enemy comes, you hold the rear of your army like a hill across a wide river, the poet tells the chief, a moment of your leisure is always hard to find, but my family's distress is great, so give the gift now; and may your strength, unshaken by foes like the great murukku post at which the young Kosar of victorious spears practise their throws, live long.
nuance: The praise is also the excuse: because the chief is always at the front or the rear of battle, the bard cannot wait for the proper moment (செவ்வி) and asks at once. The Kosar's target post makes his strength something that takes every blow and does not fall.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard presses for his gift

comparisons.tenor: the chief holding his army's rear
the chief's strength, struck by foes and unshaken

reading: The poet warns the enemy to keep clear of Pittan of the sharp spear, lord of a hill country of little villages with gooseberry fences stripped by wild cows and pebbled yards, where among bowmen who live by the bow the drum of the low-born drummer, struck till his dark hand reddens, echoes the owl in tiger-haunted heights; he gives the dancing women pearls from elephants' tusks and feeds the bards strong toddy, gentle to those who long for him, but to his foes he is like the anvil stone that takes the blows of the dark-handed smith's hammer.
nuance: The simile turns on the anvil: what bears the hammer is what shapes the iron, so the enemy who strikes him breaks himself. The poem names the drummer by his low birth (இழிபிறப்பாளன்), a rare plain statement of rank in the hill village.

thinai_evidence.note: a warning to enemies about a chief's strength

comparisons.tenor: Pittan as his enemies meet him

reading: Whether we go today, after a short while, or day after day, Kotran gives, never saying he gave before, and fills our empty vessels as we wish; may he finish the hard work his overlord wants; whether one asks for herds of fierce bulls with their stalls, heaps of threshed paddy or jewels with elephants, he gives, and gives to others as well; so may not even a thorn hurt the sole of our lord's foot, and in this world where givers are rare may his feet live so that those who live may live.
nuance: The giver is measured by repetition: going daily and being met as on the first day. The wish that his overlord's work be done ties the bards' gifts to the chief's service of his king.

thinai_evidence.note: a chief's habitual giving is described and blessed

reading: Set the pot on the fire, cook the rice, see the toddy does not run short, let the dancing women with bright jewels put on garlands, do all such things without worrying about the next meal, for Pittan of the strong horses lives, lord of the hard country where the fire set to guard the hill paddy dies down and bright gems drive off the thick dark; may his spear that wins hard battles, the great giving of his overlord Kothai, and even the hostile kings live long.
nuance: The blessing takes in the enemy kings: while they live, Pittan has wars to win and spoils to give, so the feast in the first lines depends on them.

thinai_evidence.note: the bards' household feasts on the strength of a giver

reading: May Pannan live as many days as I live; bards, see the trouble of his household: the noise of eating sounds like birds clamouring in a fruiting tree, and children of his large kin go about with rice in their hands like the thin line of tiny ants that carry their eggs to high ground before sure rain; we see it, and yet we ask again and again: is the house of the physician of hunger near or far? Tell us.
nuance: The speaker is a Chola king who wishes his own years on a small-village chief and plays a lost suppliant asking the way; the question is feigned, since the crowds with rice in hand already show the road. The hardship (இடும்பை) of the household is its press of guests.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief as the healer of hunger

comparisons.tenor: the noise of eating at Pannan's house
the children walking with rice in hand

reading: As the god of dark hue brought back the sun when the asuras hid it and the world lay in darkness, so, when the rich Kaveri country had lost its king, the chief showed the moon-white umbrella of the great Valavan, who had stayed in the hard refuge on Mullur, the hill truthful-tongued Kapilan sang, and set it up anew; and now that his famed elder has gone to the world above to enjoy the good he did here, he has appeared to end the grief of hearts searching every road, like thunder-rain that pours after a long summer has cracked the stones, scorched the forest and dried the ponds.
nuance: The poem cites an earlier poem: Mullur is the hill Kapilan sang, so the chief's house carries a fame already made in verse. Both similes (the sun restored, rain after drought) are about restoring what was lost, once for the Chola kingdom, once for the chief's own people.

thinai_evidence.note: the deed praised is restoring a king's umbrella

comparisons.tenor: the chief who restored the Chola king
the chief's coming, ending his people's grief

reading: My lord Athanungan, those who open my heart will find you there; if ever I forget you, it will be when I forget myself, when life leaves my body, you who every day take up the protection of many, like the wide sun's orb that stands at the rock pass the Moriyar, with their sky-touching umbrellas and bannered chariots, cut for the wheels of their chariots to roll through.
nuance: Gratitude is made bodily (open my heart and you are there) and is bounded by life itself, not by any later birth. The Mauryan road cut through the rock serves as a figure for what stays fixed and open to all.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron who protects many

reading: Blessed be the fate that joined me to Nalliyakkodan, lord of great Ilangai with its loud sluices, where girls at play scratching the mud a boar has ploughed find a turtle's rank-smelling eggs with honey-scented lily roots, a giver to those who lack even a small lute; my heart grieves for the days I let pass without seeing him, like people who scorned the cool clear springs of Pari's Parambu because they were in their own town, and thinks of him each time it sees his gentle nature.
nuance: The regret is for a giver who was always near: the springs of Parambu were proverbial for never failing, and their very constancy is why those beside them did not value them.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron of bards

comparisons.tenor: the poet, who let days pass without seeing a patron close at hand

reading: The gold-decked elephant a bard wins by singing, after waiting many lean days at the bright towns of sword-bearing kings, is not worth as much as the meal at great dawn in the Kudanadu of Athi, whose men, tired of sour kalaa and thudari berries, climb the river's sandbank to pick black jambu fruit, and who, among clustered little forts that let in all who are friends and not even the moonlight if foes, has the white rice thick with the fat of porcupine meat brought by the Eyinar poured without stint for all comers, eaten from big palm-leaf cups.
nuance: The comparison runs against the bard's own trade: the king's elephant, won after waiting and hunger, is worth less than a hill chief's rice given at once to anyone who comes. The forts that open to friends and shut even the moon to foes give his hospitality its edge.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a chief's open table

comparisons.tenor: Athi's dawn meal, ranked above a king's gift

patron: பாண்டியன் கீரஞ்சாத்தன் பாண்டிக் குதிரைச் சாக்கையன் எனவும் பாடம்
reading: Saththan of great name, in whose sanded yard elephants weary of the post sigh and horses tire of the stable, swears an oath with the worthy who enter and begs them to eat even when they will not; but he is not only gentle here: in the fearful battle where the weapons of foes are tangled, when the little men who made tall boasts in their own villages with cups of toddy forget them and run in fear, he goes forward and becomes their shelter.
nuance: The poem sets the oath he swears to make guests eat beside the boasts the toddy drinkers forget: one man's word at home is kept in battle, the others' is not.

thinai_evidence.note: a man's valour in covering the fleeing

poet: வடநெடுந்தத்தனார்; வடம நெடுந்தத்தனார் எனவும், வடம நெடுந்தச்சனார் எனவும் பாடம்
reading: When the generous of the earth had died and my begging bowl lay upturned, unfilled, I asked who would fill it, and many named Nagan, lord of Nalai, the soldier of the Pandya who took many lands with tight-strung drums: where an army is wanted he gives his sword, where counsel is wanted his wisdom, a manly heart that never tires under the yoke of what his king wants, of unbeaten fame, whose good battles end the kites' hunger.
nuance: The poem is shaped as a bard's search for a giver, with the praise of the soldier given as the answer others offered; the colophon files it under valour, but its frame is the upturned begging bowl.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem's act is a bard asking who will fill his bowl

reading: He has no wealth to give without end, nor the meanness to refuse saying he has none; bearing his king's troubles, the wounds that tasted iron in battle have healed and his body is so crossed with sword scars, like a tree cut again and again for medicine, that it is shaped of scars; he lives at Eernthai, enemy of the bards' hunger: old-tongued suppliant, if you want your want ended, come with us, for when we ask him he points to our unfed bellies and asks the dark-handed smith of his town to forge him a long leaf-bladed spear.
nuance: The patron is poor, and his gift is a raid: the bards' hunger is shown to the smith, not to a treasury. The scars and the spear make giving the direct fruit of fighting.

thinai_evidence.note: one bard guides another to a giver

comparisons.tenor: Maran, the enemy of the bards' hunger

title: புறநானூறு 181-200
theme: Poems 181-200 are mostly maxims on what keeps the world, a land, a king and a life worth while: the selfless, learning above birth, measured levies, good men, giving, steady friends and equanimity before fate. They end with bards' poems on asking and giving that test those maxims on real patrons.
source_issues: 186: the colophon thurai carries a modern editorial sentence after பொருண்மொழிக் காஞ்சி (ending in a stray closing parenthesis); copied exactly as the check requires, but it is not part of the colophon and should be removed from the core record.
200: the colophon thurai reads பரசிற்றுறை, a misprint for பரிசிற்றுறை; corrected in puram_thurai name.
200: text, poet, patron, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition (show reports FILLED_FROM_DURAISAMY_PILLAI); marked as it stands.
194: poet, thinai and thurai are filled from Duraisamy Pillai's edition.

183 and 187: the review's line table says sangamtamil.com lacks our opening line(s) (183 line 1; 187 lines 1-2). Our line 1 of 183 states the conditions of learning that line 2 completes, and 187's four lines form a complete poem (the four kinds of ground, then the address to the land), so the differences look like line-breaking or omission on the site; all lines are marked.
195 line 1 (பல்சான் றீரே! பல்சான் றீரே!) is flagged as repeated in 246 and 301; it is a formula of address, not a copying error.
198 line 26: வடியுறை looks like அடியுறை (one who dwells at your feet) joined to the preceding word in sandhi; the sense is clear, the spelling is unusual.

reading: A poet sends a hungry bard straight to Pannan, the true-sworded lord of a harsh, fenced forest country, telling him to go at once and show his hunger before Pannan rides out to enemy land.
nuance: The opening picture of the hunters' settlement, where the woman's son and a forest elephant's calf go after the same fallen wood-apple, is both a sign of a wild, unploughed land and of a lord whose people live without fear; the urgency of இன்னே and the timing clause (before he goes to the enemy's land) make the patron's generosity a thing that can be missed. Who takes the fruit in lines 1 to 3 is not certain from the syntax.

thinai_evidence.note: the act of the poem is directing a starving bard to a giver, which is guide-poem praise, though the colophon files it under valour

reading: The world goes on only because there are people who would not eat even the gods' nectar alone, who are without anger or sloth, fear what others fear, give their lives for honour and refuse the whole world if it comes with blame, and strive not for themselves but for others.
nuance: The poem is a single sentence that holds its subject back to the last line: the list of refusals comes first and only then does it say who these people are. The poet is a Pandya prince, so the claim that the world rests on the selfless comes from a ruler, not a supplicant.

thinai_evidence.note: a general truth about what sustains the world, addressed to no one

reading: Learning is good even at the cost of serving and paying the teacher and not resenting the lower place: a mother's heart leans to the more accomplished of her own children, a king takes counsel from the wise brother rather than the eldest, and when a man of the lowest of the four orders learns, a man of the highest comes to him.
nuance: Three hierarchies are tested in turn, the family, the royal house and the four orders, and in each learning wins over birth order or birth rank. The poet is a king, Nedunchezhiyan, so the poem concedes that even the throne's counsel follows learning. The hierarchies are named, not abolished.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem praises learning as an excellence that overturns rank, the kind of praise of a calling the Tholkappiyam puts under vaakai

reading: If a king takes his due as an elephant is fed ripe paddy cut into balls, even a small field lasts many days and the country thrives, but if a weak king with a noisy, unruly retinue grabs what he can, he is like an elephant let loose in a field that tramples more than it eats: he goes hungry and the land is ruined.
nuance: The argument is made to the king's own interest, not the subject's: greed leaves the king himself unfed (தானும் உண்ணான்). The blame falls partly on the retinue that does not know order (வரிசை அறியா), so the weak king is the one who cannot restrain those around him.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel spoken to a king, the admonition the Tholkappiyam counts under praise

comparisons.tenor: the wise king who levies by measure
the realm stripped by a greedy king and his retinue

reading: The realm is a cart of protection running on wheel and axle: if its driver is skilled it goes smoothly without harm, but if he cannot steer it sinks daily in the mire of enmity and brings one great evil after another.
nuance: The poet is himself a king, Tondaiman Ilandiraiyan, so the image of the incompetent driver is a ruler's self-warning. The cart is protection (காவல்), not wealth or conquest: the realm exists to guard.

thinai_evidence.note: a general maxim about rule, spoken by a king and addressed to no one

comparisons.tenor: the troubles that enmity brings on a realm

tamil: நெல்லும் உயிர் அன்றே; நீரும் உயிர் அன்றே;
reading: Rice is not life and water is not life: the wide world lives by its king, so it is the duty of the king with a spear-strong army to know that he is its life.
nuance: The last clause turns praise into duty: it is not the people who must know the king is their life, but the king who must know it (அறிகை ... கடனே). Read that way, the poem binds the king rather than flattering him.

thinai_evidence.note: a statement of what the king is to the world, addressed to no hearer

reading: Be it settled country or forest, low ground or high, a land is good only where its men are good; bless you, land.
nuance: Avvaiyar names four kinds of ground, the very terms by which land is classed, only to declare them irrelevant; the landscape that orders all Sangam poetry is set aside in four short lines. The goodness is the men's, and the land is praised for reflecting it.

thinai_evidence.note: a maxim on what makes a land good, addressed to the land itself

reading: However rich a man is, with many dishes and many guests, if he has no little children who toddle up, stretch out small hands, put in, touch, bite and stir the food and scatter the ghee rice over themselves, his days of living bring him no profit.
nuance: The four verbs of line 4 are a child's whole repertoire with food, and the poem lingers on the mess before it gives its verdict. The poet is the Pandya king Arivudai Nambi, a man of the feasting wealth he says is worthless without children.

thinai_evidence.note: a general verdict on what makes a life fruitful

reading: Whether he is the sole king under the white umbrella of the sea-girt earth or an unlettered hunter who watches for game sleepless at midnight and by day, each eats one measure and wears two cloths, and all else is the same; so the use of wealth is giving, for whoever means to enjoy it all himself loses much.
nuance: The argument is from the body's limit, not from virtue or merit: a stomach takes one naazhi whatever one owns, so surplus can only be given or lost. The final line can be read either as the hoarder failing in many duties or as many things slipping from his grasp.

thinai_evidence.note: a maxim on the use of wealth, addressed to no one

reading: Let me have no friendship with the small-hearted who, like the rat that eyes a little field at harvest and stuffs its hole with curved ears of grain, only build up what they already have; let my days be joined with the strong-hearted, unflagging as the hungry tiger that will not eat a boar fallen on its left side and next day rises from its cave to bring down a great bull elephant.
nuance: The two similes are built as opposites of scale: the rat fills its hole from a small field, the tiger refuses an easy boar and hunts an elephant. The tiger's refusal of prey fallen on the left is an omen custom, and it makes the tiger's hunger a chosen one.

thinai_evidence.note: a wish about the choice of friends, a general matter

comparisons.tenor: those who only hoard what they already have
the strong-hearted who will not stoop and aim high

reading: Asked why he has no grey hair after so many years, the poet answers that his wife is excellent, his children grown, his servants of one mind with him, the king does no wrong and protects, and above all his town has many worthy men, full in learning, calm and restrained.
nuance: The answer moves outward in rings: wife, children, servants, king, and last the worthy men of the town, which the poet sets above all (அதன்தலை). Freedom from age is credited to the people one lives among, not to diet, discipline or renunciation.

thinai_evidence.note: a general account of the good life, answered to an imagined questioner

reading: Every town is ours and everyone our kin; good and ill do not come from others, nor do pain and its easing; death is nothing new, and we neither rejoice that life is sweet nor in disgust call it bitter, for we have seen through the wise that a life moves by its order like a raft carried down a great river roaring over rocks after the lightning and rain, so we do not marvel at the great and still less despise the small.
nuance: The famous first line is the conclusion of an argument, not a slogan: because good and ill are not given by others, no place is foreign and no one a stranger. The raft image keeps the agent out of view; the poem says a life follows its course (முறைவழி) but does not name who set it. The equanimity is learnt from the wise (திறவோர் காட்சியின்), not claimed as one's own discovery.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem is about meeting life and death in a world that does not stay

comparisons.tenor: a life that follows its order

reading: Like an antelope chased by one man across a long white salt plain spread like a flayed hide, one might run and escape, but the life of a household binds the legs.
nuance: The poet's name, the one-plough farmer, is taken from the poem's world, and the four lines leave unsaid what he would flee: the chase is from his troubles, and the household is both what makes him want to run and what keeps him from it.

thinai_evidence.note: a general complaint about the bonds of household life

comparisons.tenor: the wide, bare white salt plain
the man who might flee his troubles

reading: In one house the dirge drum sounds, in another the cool wedding drum throbs; the joined wear flowers while the parted weep from kohl-lined eyes: whoever made this world is surely without kindness. This world is harsh; let those who know its nature look for what is sweet.
nuance: நெய்தல் here is the drum or tune of mourning, not the shore landscape or the flower. The poem blames the maker (படைத்தோன்) outright, which is rare, and then turns from complaint to counsel: knowing the world is harsh is the ground for seeking good (இனிய), not for leaving it.

thinai_evidence.note: the world's harshness and the passing of joy into grief

reading: You many worthies with hair grey as fish bones and wrinkled cheeks, in useless old age, you will grieve when the fierce one with the sharp axe binds you: if you cannot do good, at least keep from doing harm, for that pleases everyone and is also the road to the good way.
nuance: The address பல்சான்றீரே, repeated three times, is ironic: the 'many worthies' have reached old age without doing good. Death is not named but drawn as one who carries a கணிச்சி, an axe. The advice sets a floor, not a summit: refraining from harm is offered as already a way to the good.

thinai_evidence.note: old age and death held up to the living, the theme the Tholkappiyam gives to kaanchi

reading: To say yes to what one can give and no to what one cannot are both proper ways of a giver's friendship, but to promise what one cannot and refuse what one can both wound the asker and lessen the giver's fame; I have seen it now, so may your sons be well, and I, not shrinking from sun or dew, will go home to my poor shelter thinking of my faithful, bright-browed wife.
nuance: The rebuke is framed as a general rule of four cases before it becomes personal, and the poet's parting blessing on the king's sons keeps the rebuke from becoming a curse. The sense of கல்குயின்றன்ன, describing his shelter, is not secure.

thinai_evidence.note: the poem speaks to a patron about how a giver must answer a suppliant

comparisons.tenor: the poet's poor shelter from the wind

tamil: உள்ளுதும், பெரும! யாம், உவந்து நனி பெரிதே!
reading: We do not marvel at the white-umbrella wealth of kings with wind-swift horses, bannered chariots, sea-wide armies, hill-rivalling elephants and thunder-loud drums; we marvel at small-village chiefs who, though they eat only greens and varagu rice, know how to treat us; we think nothing of the riches of the unfeeling, and think of the poverty of the wise with great joy, lord.
nuance: Spoken to a great Chola king, the poem is a refusal and a warning in the form of praise of others: the grand catalogue of lines 1 to 8 is built up only to be dismissed. The small chief's meal is described with care (greens the goats have left, millet from dry land), and the point is that he knows the poet's worth (பாடறிந்து).

thinai_evidence.note: a poet speaks to a king about whom poets honour

reading: Having blessed the king's sons, born of his chaste, god-like queen, and seen his wealth, like that of the god under the banyan, the poet takes leave wishing the sons to be like their ancestors who filled the palace with enemies' treasure, and the king to live on, his days more than the sea's water, its sand and the sky's rain, while the poet in his distant land, like the bird that longs for a raindrop, waits for his grace: 'Maran, do not forget me.'
nuance: The poem is a leave-taking, not a thanks: the poet says his heart, which cries out even in dreams for lack of the king's favour, rejoiced in seeing his wealth (ஏமாந்து உவப்ப), and his last words ask not to be forgotten, so the gift is still awaited. The bird that lives on raindrops makes his waiting a matter of nature, not of choice.

thinai_evidence.note: praise and blessing of a king by a departing poet

comparisons.tenor: the king's sons, like him in might
the king's sons, who should be as their ancestors

comparisons.vehicle: பெருங்கடல் நீரினும், அக்கடல் மணலினும், நீண்டுஉயர் வானத்து உறையினும்

comparisons.tenor: the poet longing for the king's grace

reading: A noisy flock of birds does not say 'we ate yesterday' but keeps returning to the many fruits of the wide-branched banyan where a god dwells; so are suppliants, and the wealth of the generous men who welcome them is the suppliants' wealth, their want the suppliants' want.
nuance: The poem defends the suppliant's repeated asking by nature: birds do not count yesterday's meal. The last two lines join giver and asker in one fortune, so the patron's poverty would be the poet's poverty too; asking is made a bond, not a debt.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of givers through the conduct of suppliants

comparisons.tenor: suppliants who return to a patron without shame

reading: Kapilar addresses Vichikko, lord of high hills where monkeys feast on jackfruit and sleep on bamboo, a king with a fat-eating spear and fierce elephants: these are the daughters of Pari, who gave his tall belled chariot to a jasmine creeper though it never sang for him; I am a suppliant and a brahmin; take them as I give them, lord of a land of unfailing harvests.
nuance: The bard offers the daughters as a gift he himself makes (கொடுப்பக் கொண்மதி), claiming the standing of brahmin and suppliant. Pari's gift to the jasmine is invoked to show what kind of father the girls had, generous even to a creeper that could not praise him. The monkey and his mate in the hill-description may be read as a hint at the marriage proposed, but nothing in the poem states it, so it is left as scene.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard addresses a king, praising him and his dead patron

title: புறநானூறு 201-220
theme: Poems 201 to 220 are of two kinds. 201 to 211 are bards' gift poems that test the terms of patronage: a poet offering a dead patron's daughters, poets leaving patrons who gave without regard or kept them waiting, and the bard's household as evidence. 212 to 220 follow Kopperuncholan and his unseen friend Pisirandhaiyar from praise and counsel through the king's resolve to die to the laments for him.
source_issues: 203 line 4: எம்ம்னோர் is a misprint for எம்மனோர்.
206 line 7: அறி யலன்கோல் is a misprint for அறியலன்கொல் (the parallel of என்னறி யலன்கொல் in the same line); line 8: பகழும் is a misprint for புகழும்.

209 line 7: உகத்து. carries a stray full stop and may be a misprint for உகந்து; line 9 ends in a stray full stop. Line 10 is the edition variant the flag records (one edition lacks it), so our text has 19 lines where the review's table counted 18.
201 line 2: the comma is misplaced (அருளித் ,தேருடன்); line 15 is repeated in 202 line 10 (spelt மா அல் and மாஅல்), a formula for Irungovel, not a copying error.
210 line 9: a closing quotation mark ends the wife's speech but no opening mark begins it (it starts at line 5).
214 line 13: the poem ends with a comma (தவத் தலையே,) rather than a close.
218: the poet field reads கண்ணகனார் நத்தத்தனார் எனவும் பாடம், a variant note in the poet field; the review notes the site lacks our line 1, which the simile needs, so all lines are marked.
219: the poet field பெருஞ்கருவூர்ப்சதுக்கத்துப் பூதநாதனார் is misprinted (பெருங்கருவூர்ச் சதுக்கத்துப்).
220 line 1: பெருங்சோறு is a misprint for பெருஞ்சோறு.
213: the colophon thurai துணை வஞ்சி is written as two words; puram_thurai name normalised to துணைவஞ்சி.

reading: Kapilar tells Irungovel that the girls with him are the daughters of Pari of Parambu, who gave his chariot to a jasmine creeper, that he himself, a brahmin poet and their father's friend, has brought them, and asks the lord of Thuvarai, chief of forty-nine generations of Velir, to take them as his gift.
nuance: The poet makes the girls his own gift (யான்தர), so a request for a bridegroom is cast in the form of a bard's giving; the two lineages are set side by side, Pari's fame for an absurdly generous gift against Irungovel's descent from the sage's pit and forty-nine generations. Pari's death is never said: the orphaning is carried by யானே தந்தை தோழன், I am the father's friend.

thinai_evidence.note: an offer made to a named chief, carried by praise of his lineage and his giving

tamil: நீடு நிலை அரையத்துக் கேடும் கேள், இனி;
reading: After the chief has declined, Kapilar reminds him that his ancestors' town Araiyam, rich with wealth heaped in crores, fell because one of them scorned a poem by a wise man of his own kind, then asks pardon for his own foolish words offering Pari's daughters to Evvi's old clan, says he has let the matter go, and wishes the chief's spear victory.
nuance: The refusal is never stated; it is read from the poet asking pardon for his own words and saying he has let the girls go. The story of Araiyam is a threat dressed as history: a house that once scorned a poet fell. Reading கழாஅத் தலையை as the name of the scorned poet is ours.

thinai_evidence.note: a poet's parting address to a chief who refused him, closing in a blessing

comparisons.tenor: the boulder strewn with fallen vengai flowers

reading: Just as no living thing can live when the sky stops raining and the land hides its yield, it is cruel when a patron answers a bard's 'give again' with 'you took before'; worse than being unable to fill want is to kill the hope of those who come; you are not like that, generous lord who hands bards the enemy's fort as theirs before you take it, since protecting suppliants is your bounden duty.
nuance: The poem argues from rain: a sky that stopped because it had already rained would kill all life, so 'you took before' is no reason to refuse. The bard's due is called a debt (பாண்கடன்) and protection of suppliants an ornament the king is bound to wear (பூண்கடன்).

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a giver framed as a plea against refusal

comparisons.tenor: a patron who refuses the bards who come again

reading: To say 'give' is low and to refuse is lower still; to say 'take' and give is high and to refuse what is offered higher still; the thirsty do not drink from the clear wide sea but find many paths to a drinking pool, however muddied by cattle and beasts; those who come in hope blame the omens and the hour, never the giver, so I am not angry, Ori, giver who pours like the rain cloud without limit.
nuance: The four-step ladder makes refusing a gift the highest act, which quietly ranks the proud bard above the giver. The poet also gives himself a rule of conduct: a disappointed suppliant blames birds and the hour, not the patron.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a named giver after a delay

comparisons.tenor: a great but closed patron set against a small one who gives

reading: Even from the three crowned kings of full fortune we do not want gifts given without regard; hunter lord of Kodai, with strong bow and fierce hounds that cut down herds of deer, be free of harm; as the great clouds that gather over the sea do not leave without water, the bards' kin do not leave you without chariots and bright-tusked elephants.
nuance: The poem opens with a condition before any praise: honour first, gift second. The cloud image runs the usual figure backwards, since here the bards are the clouds that draw water from the patron's sea.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a patron through the bard's terms for accepting a gift

comparisons.tenor: the bards' kin who never leave the patron empty-handed

reading: Gatekeeper who never shuts the gate on bards who sow bright words in givers' ears: does Anji not know himself, or not know me? The world is not left empty when men of learning and fame die, so we have shouldered our instruments and packed our bags; like the skilled sons of a woodcutting carpenter in a forest, wherever we go, there is rice.
nuance: The address is to the gatekeeper, not the king, so the reproach reaches Anji at one remove. The phrase 'he does not know me' sets the bard's rank (வரிசை) against the patron's, and the carpenter's sons make the bard a craftsman who can earn anywhere, not a beggar.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's proud leave-taking at a patron's gate

comparisons.tenor: the bards who find a living in any land

reading: Rise, my heart, let us go: who would call them other than witless, those who see us close yet act as though they did not, and give a gift that does not gladden the heart, with a fallen face? The world is wide and providers many for those who want the honour of 'come'; only those whose spirit sinks, unlike the strong lion, pine over a hard fruit that will never ripen.
nuance: The poem distinguishes a gift that makes the face move from one that makes the heart glad (அகம்நக ... முகன்அழி), and the bard refuses the first. The poet speaks to his own heart, as akam speakers do, but the matter is the bard's honour.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard turning from a patron who gave without warmth

comparisons.tenor: the bard who leaves with spirit unbroken

reading: When I came past many hills and stood saying I had come to take a gift and go, the guardian sent it out without seeing me, saying 'take this and go'; how did he come to know me? I am not a trading bard for a thing given unseen; even a millet's worth is sweet when givers know the measure of the one they give to and give with care.
nuance: The insult is not the size of the gift but that it was given unseen (காணாது ஈத்த): the meeting is part of the gift. The bard calls the alternative trade, so a gift without recognition is a sale.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard rejecting a gift sent without a meeting

reading: Lord of a gentle land of fields where the stork rests on the stack and reapers drink toddy from lily leaves and sway to the beat of the waves: like a flock that flew to the fruit tree in the mountain cleft and turns back with nothing when it is bare, shall I who came in hope singing your fame go away empty? Even if you do not give I will not grieve; be well, and may we meet close, at your court of joy where women watch your chest broad as a hill.
nuance: The bird simile puts the fault on the bare tree, not the birds, so the patron is told he has gone barren; the refusal to grieve (இரங்குவென் அல்லேன்) and the closing blessing keep the reproach courteous.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard pressing a patron for a delayed gift

comparisons.tenor: the bard leaving the patron empty-handed

tamil: பிறனா யினன்கொல்? இறீஇயர், என் உயிர்!’ என
reading: If kings like you, ignoring your duty to protect the people, are loveless and unjust, our kind should not be born here; my faultless wife, saying that if I were even barely alive I would not fail to think of her and wondering whether unjust Death has made me another's, lives in grief, and to end her pain I give up this waiting; live long, lord: look, I go with a sad heart, my loneliness before me like the guarded fort of your enemies once you have broken it.
nuance: The wife's words are quoted inside the bard's, so the reproach to the king is spoken by a woman at home who thinks her husband dead. The final simile is double-edged: the bard is as helpless as the king's beaten enemies, which ranks him with those the king defeats.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard giving up his wait at a patron's court

reading: Lord whose army crosses with drums that roar like thunder that splits a snake's head and shakes the hills: when men who would not give said 'he bows to you because you are generous', you achieved your aim; you showed the gift as if it were in my hand and then stood by a lie; though you feel no shame I have said what should shame you, praised you till my tongue ached, worshipped your chest that took fame from being sung, and I go to my bright-browed wife, in a house where even the rat has died for lack of grain, with a son who has forgotten the breast for lack of milk.
nuance: The praise is sarcasm the poet names as such (நாணக் கூறி): the king 'achieved what he intended', which was to be praised without paying. The dead house rat is the poem's measure of want, a house too poor even for vermin.

thinai_evidence.note: a bard's ironic praise of a patron who promised and did not give

comparisons.tenor: the roar of the king's drums

reading: If you ask who your king is: in a rich land of unending festivals, where field hands drink strong toddy, eat boiled tortoise and roast eel, he is the lord of Kozhi, Kopperuncholan, enemy of the hunger of the bards' kin, who joined Potthi in flawless friendship and gives us great laughter every day.
nuance: The speaker, Pisirandhaiyar of the Pandya country, calls the Chola 'our king' (எங்கோ), so the claim of the poem is friendship, not allegiance. The king is named last, after his land's food, and praised for laughter rather than for wealth or war.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a named king's land and friendship

reading: Victorious king of the white umbrella: the two who have risen against you are not old enemies, and you are not their enemy either; when you have gained fame and gone to the higher world, what you leave belongs to them; if the young men lose, to whom will your wealth be left, and if you lose to them, only blame remains to please those who scorn you; so give up your fury, rise quickly, keep without confusion the foot-shade that shelters the fallen, for the worthy of the hard-won heaven wait eagerly to receive you as their guest.
nuance: The poem never says 'your sons'; the two are only those who came against you (நின்தலை வந்த இருவரை), and the argument works by showing that every outcome is loss: if they die there is no heir, if he loses there is only disgrace. The closing turn to heaven's guests reframes withdrawal from war as the road to a hero's next world.

thinai_evidence.note: counsel to a king who has marched against those who rose against him

reading: Those whose minds hold doubt never get past asking 'shall we do good?'; the hunter of elephants gets an elephant while the hunter of quail may come home empty-handed; so if those who aim high get what their deeds earn, they may enjoy the world where no deeds are done; if there is no such joy, they may escape rebirth; and if not reborn, to plant one's fame as high as a Himalayan peak and die in a faultless body is the best.
nuance: The argument is a chain of conditionals in which each fallback still pays: heaven, release from birth, or at least lasting fame and a whole body at death. It is spoken by the king himself; the colophon records his authorship, and the poem reads as a reason for the resolve the next poems mourn.

thinai_evidence.note: a king's reasoning about deeds and death, the matter of kaanchi rather than general counsel

comparisons.tenor: those who aim at high deeds and those who aim low

reading: In the fine land of the southern hill-lord, where bean-pickers eat their fill of the sour gruel the herd-woman cooks from forked-ear varagu with white velai flowers and white curd, lives Pisiron, they say, the guardian of my life; he may stay away in times of wealth, but in times of trouble he will not stay away.
nuance: The king, about to die, praises a poet he has never met as the keeper of his life, and the proof offered is a prediction. The plain mullai food of the friend's land answers the toddy and eel of 212, so each friend praises the other through what is eaten at home.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of a friend through his land and his loyalty

reading: Do not doubt, wise men, saying that though friends by hearing alone, never having met in many years, it is hard for him to act on it now; he is without scorn, sweet, bound in friendship, wants no lie that would spoil his fame, and when he names himself he says 'my name is the foolish Chola', so close is his claim; he will not stay away at such a time; he will come now; keep his place.
nuance: Friendship without meeting is the poem's claim and its wager: the king orders a seat kept for a man he has never seen. The friend's taking the king's own name (பேதைச் சோழன்) is offered as the sign of the bond; that he speaks of the king as 'foolish' is affection, and our reading of who says the name follows the line as it stands.

thinai_evidence.note: praise of an absent friend's faithfulness

reading: It is a wonder that a king of such great glory should resolve on this here; a greater wonder that a worthy man of renown from another land should come here at such a time, fame his tradition and friendship his pillar; the greatness of the king who said 'he will come' and the wisdom of the man who came without fail grow past wonder the more one wonders; so what will become of this world that has lost the one who won the heart of a worthy man living where his sceptre did not reach? It is to be pitied.
nuance: Three wonders are stacked: the king's resolve, the friend's arrival, and the fulfilled prediction; the lament comes only in the last two lines. The poem treats the friend's coming as the proof of the king's worth: he won a heart beyond the reach of his rule.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead king, the matter of kaanchi

reading: Gold, coral, pearl and the lovely gem of the great hill, though they come from far apart, come together in one place when a precious jewel is strung; so the worthy always fall to the side of the worthy, and the unworthy to the unworthy.
nuance: Read in its place after 215 to 217, the jewel stands for the Chola and the Pandya-country poet joined at the end; the poem itself names no one, and its second half (the unworthy join the unworthy) gives the maxim an edge against those who stayed away.

thinai_evidence.note: a general truth drawn from an event, with no lament in the words

comparisons.tenor: the worthy drawn together from distant places

reading: Warrior who dries out your whole strong body in the dappled shade on the fork of the river island, you are vexed with me; many indeed are those who sat with you in your resolve.
nuance: The four lines carry the whole scene by implication: the king sits on the river island wasting away, others have already joined him, and the poet, arriving late, reads the king's displeasure as being with him. குறிஇருந்தோர் is read as those who sat by his purpose.

thinai_evidence.note: a late-comer's words to a king fasting to death

reading: Like the grieving mahout who lost the great tusker that brought him plenty of food and kept him for many years, and weeps to see the empty post in the shed where it stood, was I not shaken when I saw the assembly hall of the famous old town that Killi, giver of chariots with golden garland, has left?
nuance: The mahout was fed by the elephant (பெருஞ்சோறு பயந்து), so the simile casts the king as the provider and the poet as his dependant; the empty post (வெளில்) and the empty assembly (மன்றம்) are the poem's two images of absence.

thinai_evidence.note: a lament for a dead king, the matter of kaanchi

comparisons.tenor: the poet before the empty hall of the dead king

title: புறநானூறு 221-240
theme: Poems 221-240 are all laments (kaiyarunilai) for dead patrons: Pothiyar's three for Kopperunchozhan, whose friend was told to follow later and who as a hero-stone still makes room for old friends; laments for Karikalan, Nalankilli and Killi Valavan that reproach Death as a fool who ate its own seed or a suppliant who had to beg; the potter asked for an urn as big as the earth; Avvai's laments for Anji, his pyre, his hero-stone and the toddy he shared; poems for Evvi, Pari, Ilaveliman, Nambi Nedunchezhiyan and Aay, ending in the bard's resolve to seek a new patron and the scattering of poets to other lands.
source_issues: 221 line 8: உய்த்த்ன்று is a misprint for உய்த்தன்று.
224 line 4: கணட is a misprint for கண்ட.
225 line 1: தீங்சோறு is a misprint for தீஞ்சோறு.
228 line 1: கலங்செய் (second time) is a misprint for கலஞ்செய்; line 13: அயின் is a misprint for ஆயின்.
230: the colophon thurai reads கையுறுநிலை, a misprint for கையறுநிலை; copied as it stands, corrected in puram_thurai.
230: the review's line table reports a line-break difference (site 16 lines, ours 15); our current text has 16 lines and reads complete, so all lines are marked.
232 line 4: கொல்லொ is a misprint for கொல்லோ; line 6: கொடுப்புவும் is a misprint for கொடுப்பவும்.
232: the colophon gives two thinais (பொதுவியல்; தும்பை) and two thurais (கையறுநிலை; பாண்பாட்டும் ஆம்); copied as they stand, both thurais in puram_thurai.
233 line 8: வைகறு is probably a misprint for வைகுறு (dawn).
235: the review's line table says we lack a site line 11; our current text has 20 lines and the spear passage (lines 10 to 15) reads continuously, so nothing is flagged as missing.
236: the colophon patron is None, though the poem names பாரி (line 3), Kapilar's well-known patron.
238 line 11: ஆகுல அதற்படல் looks corrupt; the reading is uncertain.
239 line 1: மணந்தணன் is a misprint for மணந்தனன்.
229: the review notes the site gives a different thurai label; our colophon's கையறுநிலை fits the poem, which mourns the king after an omen.
225 line 7 is repeated as 237 line 13 (and 245 line 3), as show flags; it is a formula for the cremation ground and is marked in each poem.

Thinai: every poem's colophon has பொதுவியல்; we infer kaanchi for all twenty, since the Tholkappiyam places the lament of those left behind (கையறுநிலை) under kaanchi (porul 2.19); the disagreement is one of scheme, not of reading.

reading: The poet lists what the dead king was: fame given to singers, love given to dancers, a just sceptre praised by the virtuous, firm friendship praised by the able, gentleness to women and strength to men, a home for the learned; Death, which does not weigh such worth, took his life, so he calls the truthful poets to come, hold the grieving kin, and revile Death, saying the patron has become a hero-stone wearing unfading fame while the wide world hangs in sorrow.
nuance: The catalogue of six balanced half-lines is undone by one word, நினையாக் கூற்றம்: Death is blamed not for cruelty but for not thinking, for failing to weigh the very qualities the poem has just counted. The patron's end is a stone that wears fame like a garland (சூடி).

thinai_evidence.note: it laments a patron taken by Death and turned into a hero-stone, the matter of kaanchi's kaiyarunilai (porul 2.19)

reading: Speaking to the dead king, the poet recalls that he was told to come only after the famous son had been born to the king's wife, she who wears flame-bright jewels and never leaves him even as his shadow, and so was left behind here; he calls the king loveless and asks what place he now has, since the king, a lover of fame, is not one to sit without thinking of him.
nuance: The poem does not name what the king was doing or what 'come' meant; read with 223 and the colophon's patron, the summons is to join him in his chosen death, so 'loveless' is a friend's reproach for being kept from dying with him, and the son's birth is the duty that held the poet back.

thinai_evidence.note: the friend left behind by a dead king laments his own exclusion, a kaanchi kaiyarunilai

comparisons.tenor: the wife's constancy to the king

reading: Having been shade to many and praised high by the world, the king, unable to go on, folded into a narrow place; yet even now that he has become an enduring hero-stone, he surely gives room and welcome to the old friends of long intimacy, whose bond is as close as life's love for the body, if they go to him.
nuance: The hospitality the king showed alive (இடங் கொடுத்து அளிப்ப) is credited to the stone, so the friends who follow him in death are pictured as guests arriving at his gate; line 2 (தலைப்போ கன்மையிற் சிறுவழி மடங்கி) is compressed and may describe his last confinement rather than the stone's narrow site.
